#2810. Frustrated Jordan Poole open to Bay Area return after 51-point loss to Warriors

SAN FRANCISCO ― Jordan Poole helped the Golden State Warriors win an NBA championship in 2022, but it hasn't always gone well for Poole since leaving the Bay Area via trade in 2023.

That was certainly true in his return Monday night.

The Warriors delivered a 51-point beatdown Nov. 9 against the Pelicans, defeating them 138-87 at Chase Center. After the game, Poole sounded off after his Pelicans dropped to 4-7.

"Pretty (expletive) difficult. Pretty (expletive) difficult," Poole told reporters. He also reminisced about better days in the Bay Area.

"I mean you just played right. They played the right way, bro. They played good basketball. They played team basketball," Poole said. "Obviously, the environment is pretty high level. But like I said, once you put a lot of work and you got hardware with an organization, with a team, with a city, you're kind of cemented in the history. So it's good, but do I miss it? Hell yeah!"

Poole, who finished with seven points on 1-of-5 field goals with three rebounds and two assists, is averaging just 6.2 points on 19% shooting from the field and 23.5% on 3-point attempts.

That's a long way from his best season with Golden State during 2022-23, when he averaged 20.4 points.

Poole, who had a reunion with former backcourt mate Stephen Curry before tip-off, said after the game that he'd absolutely welcome an official reunion back to the Bay.

"Yes. I mean, it feels like home, though," Poole said. "Driving into the (expletive) arena, you know, crossing the the Bay Bridge or wherever you're coming from, it definitely feels natural. And I think it's pretty evident, you know, the way that I play is very fitting to how I used to play here. Nothing's changed, you know, other than the system that I'm in.

"We won a championship, you know, so it works. And it did work," he added. "That's what you ultimately want to do when you come out here and you play the game. So, to answer your question, definitely. This is my last year on the deal (in New Orleans). I'm a free agent at the end of the season, so you never really know what's gonna happen."

Such a return might mean reuniting with Draymond Green. A leaked video in 2022 showed Green punch Poole during a practice that season. The Warriors traded Poole the following year. Green, who is also in the final year of his contract, wasn't opposed to a reunion.

"That would be incredible," Green said according to the Mercury News. "I have no issue with that at all. I will never stand in the way of this organization thinking they can better themselves. The issue will never be me. Ever."

Poole is in the final year of a four-year, $128 million contract, he signed with the Warriors before being traded to the Wizards. Poole is owed $34 million this season and then he will become an unrestricted free agent in the summer of 2027. He said if there's any place he's comfortable playing, it's where it all started in the Bay Area.

"I always love coming back to the Bay. Definitely feels like home," Poole said. "The fans are always really welcoming. Always cool to see some jerseys and fans I used to see her all the time, so it's definitely a warm welcome, and I definitely miss it for sure."

Poole was drafted by the Warriors with the 28th overall pick in the 2019 NBA Draft, becoming a champion and a fan favorite in the Bay Area.

The Pelicans' last winning season was the 2023–24 season, when they finished with a record of 49–33. Poole, then, played for the Washington Wizards, who finished 15–67.

"It's only so much that you can control. You know what I mean?" Poole said. "I think over the last probably last few seasons, I think I've had five coaches in four years, and it's a tough recipe to be successful. And different organizations trying to figure out what they want to do with the team. Multiple front offices, so it's just been a lot of moving parts."

A lot of Poole's frustration stems from leaving a winning culture with the Warriors for franchises struggling to find their identity.

"Coming from a team that had one common goal, knew we wanted to win. Everybody's on the same page. Everybody came into camp trying to win a championship, ready to sacrifice playing team ball," Poole said. "That's kind of like the way I grew up; was the way I played my entire career. So it's definitely different, and it's been an adjustment. But there's nothing better than playing the right way and playing team ball.

"I think tonight, just watching the game was a prime example of that," he added. "I mean, it's been pretty difficult, but you know, that's life. You have to just figure out ways to keep pushing, keep thriving, and you know, try to make the most of whatever situation you have. Keep learning."

Poole and Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg are both former Michigan Wolverines, and the two shared a moment after the game, swapping jerseys.

"We share the same alma mater. He got a championship, I told him congrats on that. We like to keep our Michigan circle pretty close-knit," Poole said. "Let him know that he has another supporter in the league. He's been playing really well and tremendous. I just want him to keep it up man. If there's anything that he needs or anything I can do to help, you know, just being a guy who's been in the league for a little bit, I just told him to reach out."

"It was amazing. I've always wanted to meet him since I went to Michigan," Lendeborg said to USA TODAY Sports about Poole. "Hearing, seeing everything he did here for Golden State, he's an phenomenal player, phenomenal person. He seems like a guy who pretty much has the same personality and character as me. It was great to meet him, he said a bunch of kind words. It was a great interaction for me."

#2808. Manchester United’s Jacob Devaney nominated for international player of the year award

Manchester United's Jacob Devaney has been nominated for an award at the 36th Football Association of Ireland (FAI) International Awards.

The youngster has been recognised for his performances in the green of Ireland and has been named to a three-man shortlist for Ireland's U21s player of the year.

He has been nominated alongside Tottenham Hotspur's (on loan at Lincoln City) Mason Melia and Wycombe Wanderers' Jamie Mullins.

The award has previously been won by Manchester United academy graduates Robbie Brady and Lee O'Connor. Perhaps the most recognisable winner of the award is Jack Grealish, who switched allegiance shortly after to represent England.

Devaney has made 12 appearances for Ireland U21s, with the most recent coming in a thrilling 3-1 victory over England that sealed a play-off berth for the 2027 U21s European Championship.

The midfielder has been named in Ireland's squad for the upcoming play-off double-header against Finland, which could see Ireland qualify for the U21s Euros for the first time ever.

He also recently captained his country in a friendly against Qatar U21s, an honour he has held with United's U21s as well.

After a stellar loan last season at St. Mirren, Devaney impressed on United's pre-season tour with a goal against Rosenborg BK but did not get a chance to show his full potential, being played out of position at centre-back rather than his more natural central midfield role.

A combative, press-resistant midfielder, Devaney's consistency and versatility make him an asset to any team and could prove important to United's lack of depth in the future.

The award nomination will provide confidence to the 19-year-old as he looks to get back on track after a rocky start to the season.

Looking to build upon his successful loan last season, Devaney returned to Scotland, moving up the table to Hibernian.

Devaney went straight into their starting XI, but a string of poor results to start the season actually sees them lying below St. Mirren in the table and, as a result, the manager who brought him to the club was sacked.

In his first appearance under the new manager, Marink Reedijk, Devaney unfortunately picked up a straight red card just seven minutes after being introduced from the bench.

To make matters worse, the red card challenge actually resulted in him getting injured, which has kept him out ever since.

The Midlothian View report that Devaney is nearing a return from injury, but he'll need to impress Reedijk, who has said, "this is the difficulty for me because I've seen Jacob for two training sessions and five minutes on the pitch in Dundee. And after that, I haven't seen him and worked with him."

"Off the pitch, I have an idea of who he is as a person. But now I also want to see how he brings this to the pitch. And this I cannot judge on yet."

Devaney's return starts with Ireland U21s, though, and a potential player of the year award which will bring him the confidence to kick on and perhaps earn a spot back at United next season.

#2807. Not many players are truly untradeable

In recent days (including today), reports have emerged that certain players will not be traded. That definitely does not mean they’re untradeable.

It means only that the team has yet to get an offer it will accept. The mere process of working the insiders to send that message could give the process one final goosing.

Regardless, not many players are truly untradeable. For all but a handful of players, there’s an offer that his current team would accept.

The only players who currently wouldn’t be traded, in our view, are Bills quarterback Josh Allen, Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow, Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes, Bears quarterback Caleb Williams, Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence, Packers quarterback Jordan Love, and probably 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy.

Any other can be had, at the right offer (up to and including three first-round picks plus more). By now, teams know whether the right offer will be made. Which makes it easy for them to throw out their chests and say the player won’t be traded.

And to reverse course if an offer they can’t refuse is made before 4:00 p.m. ET today.

#2805. What Kirk Cousins trade means to Raiders

The Las Vegas Raiders traded quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings for a 3rd round pick Tuesday. it opens the door for the Raiders play No. 1 overall draft pick Fernando Mendoza.

Here is a look at the key aspects of the decision:

Some people may have thought the Raiders could have gotten more than the Vikings' second third-round pick for a player who could potentially help them get to the Super Bowl and a player they were desperate to get. In the big picture, this is a nice get for the Raiders. They paid Cousins just $650,000 this season. They got four wins, a mentor to Mendoza and a third-round pick. Not bad.

The Raiders will have plenty of holes to fill on the roster next offseason, so adding another top 100 pick is big. They should have four now. They can use it to acquire more picks. So, this is a valuable piece.

Mendoza will face the vaunted Seattle defense in his starting debut. And the challenging defense parade will not end soon. Mendoza is being thrown to the wolves, but, clearly the Raiders believe it won't be too big for him to handle.

I'll chuckle when someone makes a clever joke about everything, but beyond that, I can't find myself getting invested in the whole thing. It's Philadelphia vs. Boston. Willis was revealed to be dealing with groin tightness during the Dolphins' Week 9 game against the Detroit Lions.

Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley acknowledged that it impacted Willis' play, and particularly his ability to run at full speed.

"It was tight today and you could see it," Hafley said of Willis' groin during a postgame news conference on Sunday, Nov. 8. "You could see he really couldn't open up. There was a couple of plays where I give him credit. He pulled it, he ran and he got us yards and he got out of trouble against a good defensive line. But you could see he just wasn't quite able to go full speed. So, we'll see how he's at tomorrow and we'll go from there."

Hafley did not provide much of an update about Willis' status during another media availability on Monday, Nov. 9, saying he hadn't yet spoken to medical staff by the time he met with reporters.

Nonetheless, the Dolphins opted to place Willis on IR on Tuesday, Nov. 10, sidelining him for at least four games. As a result, Miami will turn to its backup quarterback ahead of its Week 10 game against the Indianapolis Colts.

Kyle McCord is currently entrenched as Miami's backup quarterback. The 24-year-old joined the Dolphins on eve of the 2026 NFL season after being acquired via trade from the Green Bay Packers.

McCord was originally selected in the sixth round of the 2025 NFL Draft by the Philadelphia Eagles. He played collegiately at Ohio State and Syracuse, with his stint with the Orange helping to establish himself as a Day 3 prospect.

McCord has never played an NFL snap but he has played extensively across the 2025 and 2026 NFL preseasons. In that action, he completed 55.5% of his passes for 637 yards, five touchdowns and two interceptions while playing for the Eagles and the Packers.

The Dolphins will be hoping McCord can justify the faith the team put in him when it traded away Quinn Ewers ahead of the 2026 NFL season and brought in McCord in a separate deal.

The Dolphins have three quarterbacks in their organization. Here's a look at the pecking order within their QB room.

Cook is presently on the Dolphins' practice squad, but he could be signed to the 53-man roster with Willis out of action.

Cook spent his rookie season with the New York Jets after going undrafted and made four starts. He failed to win any of them while completing 57.5% of his passes for 739 yards, two touchdowns and seven interceptions.

It isn't clear whether the Dolphins will add a third quarterback to their organization with Willis sidelined for at least four weeks. If Miami does, it could target either Mark Gronowski or Cam Miller, who each spent part of the 2026 NFL offseason on the team's 90-man roster.

#2797. How Jayson Tatum and the Celtics haven't skipped a beat without Jaylen Brown

Despite having Jayson Tatum for a grand total of 522 minutes during the 2025-26 regular season, the Boston Celtics won nearly 70% of their games, finished in the top five in the NBA in both offensive and defensive efficiency, and landed the No. 2 seed in the Eastern Conference. They reached that level of success thanks, in large part, to Tatum's longtime running mate, Jaylen Brown, turning in the finest individual season of his career en route to a sixth-place finish in MVP voting and an All-NBA Second Team selection.

After that, though, the Celtics traded Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers this summer — a move that you might have heard just a teensy bit about over the past five months, and that has been driving no small amount of conversation ahead of the first meeting of the season between Boston and Philly on Tuesday night.

Since that tectonic roster shift, as they seek to chart a new path forward with a shuffled-up rotation and without a franchise cornerstone, the Celtics have … won 80% of their games, rank in the top seven in the NBA in both offensive and defensive efficiency, and sit in the No. 2 seed in the Eastern Conference.

The more things change, the more they stay the same?

This, to some degree, was the bet that Brad Stevens made when he made the decision to move Brown for Paul George, two first-round picks and two second-round picks. In the longer term, exchanging Brown — who has three years and $185 million remaining on his contract, and is also in line for an extension — for George — who makes less this season, has a player option for next season and comes off the books one year earlier — tidies up the Celtics' balance sheet moving forward, potentially putting them in better position to remain competitive in the race for the top of the East several years down the line. (Say it with me, Brad: "optionality!")

In the here-and-now, though, Stevens wagered that, as excellent as Brown was last season and as vital as he's been to the Celtics' perennial success for the past decade, the surrounding talent and head coach Joe Mazzulla's system would provide enough insulation to ensure that the team wouldn't skip too many beats without Brown. Through 10 games, at least? Boston looks pretty right about that.

The Celtics enter Tuesday's heavyweight battle with the Sixers looking broadly like the same elite squad they were last season. On offense, they sit in or near the top 10 in points scored and allowed per possession, and both team effective field goal percentage and opponents' eFG%. They're great at both avoiding turnovers and forcing them. They grab a ton of offensive rebounds and defend without fouling. They still jack a ton of 3s and make 'em at a top-10 clip, and still give up a ton of 3s in favor of protecting the rim without giving up the entire store on defense. They still play a methodical and effective brand of half-court basketball on offense; they're still great at preventing transition opportunities, despite sending multiple bodies to the offensive glass.

Even without Brown, the fundamentals of who the Celtics are haven't changed; the specifics of how they get there, though, are a little bit different. It starts with Tatum, now 18 months removed from rupturing his Achilles tendon and once again firmly entrenched as Boston's No. 1 option.

Tatum is still ironing out some of the wrinkles in his scoring game, finishing at substandard rates at the rim, from midrange and from beyond the 3-point arc. As he told reporters after blowing out the Charlotte Hornets last week, "I still got a little ways to to get back to being the best I ever felt."

Even with his bucket-getting lagging a bit, though, the 28-year-old is off to a flying start, averaging 27.1 points and 6 rebounds in 33.8 minutes per game. (He's been nails in crunch time, too, ranking eighth in the league in clutch scoring, with 21 points in 15 minutes on 8-for-13 shooting with 3 assists and 0 turnovers.) Just as Brown stepped into a higher-volume role in his absence last season, Tatum has slid into the monster void left by Brown's departure this season. He's finishing a career-high 33.3% of Boston's offensive possessions with a shot attempt, foul drawn or turnover, and leads the Celtics in usage, touches and time of possession.

As Gary Washburn of the Boston Globe put it, "Within the Celtics organization, there appears to be a sense of relief that the tension is gone" — that the team's hierarchy is clarified and established, with Tatum at the top of the pecking order, George comfortably slotting in behind him, and everybody else falling in line after that. Despite that, though, it hasn't felt like Tatum's got a stranglehold of Boston's offense — far from it, in fact.

Tatum's on-ball percentage — literally the share of his floor time that he has the ball in his hands — is down from where it was the past two seasons. His average time of possession of 5.1 minutes per game, 33rd in the NBA, between Donovan Mitchell and Ja Morant.

His willingness to get off the ball rather than pound it has helped produce a more egalitarian attack. Boston is averaging 27.2 assists per game, seventh-most in the NBA, up from 24.6 per game (27th) last season. Those dimes are leading to 70 points per game via assist, sixth-most in the league, up from 64 per game (22nd) last season.

Plenty of those helpers are coming directly off Tatum's fingertips. In the early going of the season, his playmaking has really leaped off the screen. Whether working in the pick-and-roll, operating out of the post, or surveying from the top of the floor at the nail, he's mapping the floor and delivering on-time and on-target feeds more often than ever. Tatum is averaging a career-high 7.8 assists against 2.8 turnovers per game, creating more baskets at the rim than all but five players in the NBA, according to PBP Stats, and setting up more 3-pointers than all but eight. He's one of just two players in the NBA in the top 10 in both scoring and assists. The other? The scorching-hot Luka Dončić.

The player Tatum has assisted the most thus far this season? George, who's been the recipient of 13 Tatum dimes, and who has looked like a hand-in-glove fit in his new digs.

George has picked up where he left off last season, when he came back from a 25-game suspension for violating the NBA/NBPA joint anti-drug program by taking "improper medication" for mental health issues to shine for the Sixers in their playoff push and their first-round victory over these same Celtics. He's averaging 20.4 points, 5.2 rebounds and 4.1 assists in 30.1 minutes per game, shooting 50.7% on 2-pointers, 42.5% on 3-pointers while taking more than eight per game, and 80.8% from the free-throw line.

The nine-time All-Star isn't quite the full-tilt offensive force that he was earlier in his career, but he's fit in brilliantly as a secondary scorer and creator who can demand attention as an off-ball threat on offense, and a high-level, gap-filling playmaker who can help crank up the heat on the defensive end. He's still capable of assuming a larger role when called upon, too: When Tatum got the night off against the Bucks last Wednesday, George stepped to the forefront, scoring 25 points with 5 assists, 4 steals and 3 rebounds to lead the way in a 109-102 win.

"The way we're asking him to play is maybe a little bit different than what he's been asked to do in the past," Mazzulla told reporters in Milwaukee on Sunday. "He enjoys that, he's open-minded to it and he just works at it. He's very hard on himself. Holds himself to a very high standard, constantly watching film, taking notes in his journal and just processing the game. He takes pride in learning and getting better, and you're seeing the fruits of that."

The C's are also seeing the fruits of swapping Brown for George in the possession game. According to Jared Dubin's tracking at Last Night in Basketball, the Celtics finished 15th in the nightly possession battle last season, barely generating more scoring chances than their opposition on a night-to-night basis despite top-five finishes in both offensive rebounding rate and offensive turnover rate — due in large part to bottom-10 marks in both getting to the free-throw line and forcing turnovers on defense. Seven of the 14 teams that finished ahead of Boston last season won a playoff series — including all four conference finalists, and the Sixers team that eliminated them in the first round of the playoffs.

It is perhaps notable, then, that the rate at which the Celtics forced turnovers last season increased more with Brown off the floor than it did for any other player who logged at least 1,000 minutes — and that their forced turnover rate had been significantly higher with him off the floor in each of the previous two seasons.

So: Out went Brown, and in came George, a superior off-ball defender who has consistently posted higher steal rates, and center Mitchell Robinson, who'd built his reputation in New York as one of the league's premier extra-possession creators on offense and a disruptive presence in the middle on defense.

Robinson hasn't yet begun to make a major impact in tilting the math. After a sluggish start to the season following the Knicks' championship run and a short summer, the new arrival has started to round into shape, though, averaging 7 points, 8 rebounds and 2.7 steals-plus-blocks over the last three games, with the C's outscoring opponents by 30 points in his 53 minutes of floor time. All told, though, the Celtics have ratcheted up their board-crashing another notch, pulling in 34% of their missed shots through 10 games, up from 31.8% last season.

They're taking 6.5 more free-throw attempts per game, too, due in large part to a more concerted effort to pressure the rim. Last season, Boston ranked dead last in the share of its field goal attempts that came within four feet of the basket. This season, that's up to 17th.

Tatum's played a big role there. Replacing Brown's high-volume attacking as the only Celtic to rank in the top 50 in the league in drives to the basket per game, he's been living at the free-throw line. His previous career high in trips to the charity stripe was 8.4 per game, accumulated when averaging 36.9 minutes a night during the 2022-23 season. Through his first nine appearances of this season, he's taking 9.3 freebies in 33.8 minutes a night — a notable uptick on a per-minute and per-possession basis, and on pace for far and away the highest free-throw attempt rate of his career. (In fact, Tatum's .477 FTA rate ranks in the top 15 in the league among all non-centers.)

Most notably, though, the C's have been significantly more disruptive on the ball. Last season, Boston ranked 28th in the NBA in steals, 25th in deflections and 23rd in opponent turnover rate, playing more conservatively on defense in the belief that if they just stayed at home, funneled the ball to the areas and shooters they preferred, and contested, the math would work out in their favor over the long run.

This season, though — owing partly to the arrival of George, who's been a demon in the passing lanes in the early going — the Celtics are tied for 14th in steals, fifth in deflections and sixth in opponent turnover rate. They're cashing in on those miscues, too, scoring 20.8 points per game off turnovers — seventh-most in the league, and a full five points per game more than last season. (It's also on pace to be more than any Celtics team has posted since Rick Pitino was on the sidelines at the Garden, regaling reporters about Larry Bird and doors.)

Add up the gains in creating cough-ups, in getting to the line and in even more aggressively crashing the offensive boards, and the Celtics are now generating 4.1 more possessions per game than their opponents — the third-highest total in the league, according to Dubin's tracking.

Thanks to Tatum's playmaking, George's shotmaking and a collective effort from a deep rotation, the Celtics have made those extra possessions count, producing a top-five offense despite shooting just 63.2% at the rim as a team (a bottom-five mark) and seeing multiple players (Tatum, Derrick White, Payton Pritchard, Baylor Scheierman, Jordan Walsh, Hugo González) struggle with frigid jumpers in the early going. If those perimeter players start to thaw out a little bit, this offense could hit a new level, and the Celtics could once again find themselves in the thick of the championship chase, even with Brown now plying his trade elsewhere in the division. The more things change, the more they stay the same.

#2794. Broncos salary cap update after acquiring Daiyan Henley's contract

Going into the 2026 NFL trade deadline, OverTheCap.com estimated the Denver Broncos had about $4.6 million in available salary cap space.

The Broncos then agreed to trade a pair of draft picks to the Los Angeles Chargers in exchange for inside linebacker Daiyan Henley. With that trade, Denver inherited what's left of the fourth and final year of Henley's rookie contract, about $1.837 million for the second half of the season.

So, after accounting for Henley's cap hit of just over $1.8 million, the Broncos have something in the ballpark of about $2,765,451 in remaining cap space this season. Denver will have to keep a cushion for potential in-season signings and the possibility of players landing on injured reserve and still counting against the cap.

Any unused salary cap space the Broncos do not use this season will roll over and add to the team's 2027 total. OTC currently projects Denver will have about $30.46 million available next offseason.

#2790. The best revenge for Jaylen Brown is to keep doing what he’s doing

Sunday wasn't the finest outing of the 2026-27 season for the Sixers.

They struggled defensively against the one-win Bulls, but came away with a 127-121 win in Chicago, moving their record to a league-best 9-2. An afternoon day game to close out a three-game road trip against a team collecting ping-pong balls is ripe for a letdown, but the Sixers took care of business.

Jaylen Brown was strong throughout, dropping a game-high 29 points to go along with seven rebounds and four assists. The five-time All-Star's numbers have been solid through 10 games with averages of 22.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.0 assists. He's shooting 47.7% from the field (the exact same percentage he shot last season) with a decent uptick from three at 39.2%.

As the Sixers get set to welcome Jayson Tatum and the Boston Celtics to South Philly on Tuesday, things remain unsettled between Brown and his former organization. When it comes to Tatum, who Brown spent nine seasons with in Boston, there is no beef, but maybe some lamb chops and gravy, as the 2024 Finals MVP put it.

With all the attention and narratives, it's hard to know what we'll see Tuesday night. Will Brown be out for revenge or does he just want to get a win for his team?

There's a way to do both — keep doing exactly what he's doing.

While the numbers have been solid, closely resembling the numbers he put up in 2023-24 when he helped the Celtics win a championship, it's been the little things with Brown.

Sunday's win was a prime example. As the plucky young Bulls kept coming, Brown provided an offensive boost, nailing a pair of threes in the fourth to thwart multiple Chicago runs. With under a minute left, he made all four of his free throws and also came away with a steal on Josh Giddey while the game remained in doubt.

Earlier last week, he made similar plays against the Pistons. While the Sixers were in control throughout the game — with Brown scoring a game-high 30 — a late comeback attempt by Cade Cunningham in Detroit was enough to make any Sixers fan nervous.

A Cunningham layup cut the lead to 106-102. After a rough offensive possession that ended in a Joel Embiid missed three, the Pistons' All-Star guard came charging up the floor. He pulled up for three in transition, but was blocked by Brown. If that shot goes in, it's suddenly a one-point game with 38 seconds left. Instead, Brown's rejection allowed the Sixers to close the game at the free throw line.

While we heard so much talk about Brown's advanced analytics and on/off splits this offseason, it's hard to quantify a guy who simply makes winning plays.

"He's a really good player," Nick Nurse said last week. "He just wins. He defends. He'll rebound. Obviously, he can score from a bunch of different levels, and I'll take all that any day. It's been phenomenal to coach him.

"What does he bring? He brings an intangible of confidence to your team. Even maybe he's not pouring in points or doing anything that you're [seeing in the box score], but there's a level of fight and competitive drive and winning spirit."

Brown has flaws like any other player. Last season, he turned the ball over more than any player in the NBA. This season, he's averaging 2.1 giveaways a game, on pace for his best season in that category since 2018-19.

There were concerns Brown wanted his own team, which supposedly led to the rift with Tatum. Thus far, there have been no issues there. In fact, Brown even openly said last week this was Tyrese Maxey's team and they're all following the second-longest-tenured Sixer's lead.

When Brown is on the floor, the Sixers' net rating is +5.4, per DataBallr. It's -3.1 when he's off. So, it's cut and dry, the Sixers are a better team when Jaylen Brown is on the court.

And just like his time with the Celtics, his current team has an excellent record.

His best path to revenge against his former team is to do what he does — win.

"Listen, the dude is tough and he wins. I'll take that all day long," Nurse said. "Makes a lot of winning plays, man. He's a winner."

#2785. Raiders rookie QB Fernando Mendoza in line to make first career start vs. Seahawks after Kirk Cousins trade

Fernando Mendoza, a reigning national champion, is poised to face the defending Super Bowl champions in his first career NFL start.

Mendoza, who led Indiana on a storybook run to College Football Playoff glory, is in line to get the nod for the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday at Allegiant Stadium against the Seattle Seahawks.

He's up for a 4-5 Raiders team that traded veteran Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings for a 2027 third-round pick hours before Tuesday's trade deadline. That deal effectively marked the beginning of the Mendoza era in Vegas.

After learning under the 38-year-old Cousins before and during the season, the 23-year-old Mendoza is set for quite the three-game test leading up to the Raiders' Week 13 bye.

Not only will he have to face the Seahawks' vaunted defense, but he'll have to go up against the Denver Broncos and Cleveland Browns the subsequent two weeks. Entering Week 10, all three of those teams rank inside the top 13 in fewest points per game allowed this season. The Broncos and Browns are tied with a handful of teams for fourth in the NFL with 26 sacks.

Mendoza has attempted only eight regular-season passes. All of those came in relief of Cousins down the stretch of a 45-17 road loss to the New England Patriots. That was part of a four-game Raiders skid that followed their head-turning 3-0 start.

First-year head coach Klint Kubiak, who named Cousins the team's Week 1 starter after evaluating both him and Mendoza in the preseason, stuck with Cousins under center despite the October losing streak.

Cousins was open throughout his stay in Las Vegas that he was well aware of the circumstances of his role and that his time as Raiders QB1 was limited. He stressed that he wanted to put the team in the best position to win games, even if that meant at some point handing the baton to Mendoza.

But Cousins played so well that he kept his job leading up to the deadline. In fact, an ESPN report surfaced this past Sunday morning, detailing how, at the time, the Raiders weren't interested in dealing him.

Cousins turned back the clock while working with Kubiak, posting a 20:8 touchdown-to-interception ratio. His 20 TD passes are good for second-most in the league and signify his first season with at least that many since his 2022 campaign with the Vikings, with whom he played from 2018-23.

Cousins turned out to be among the best NFL rentals in recent memory. The Raiders paid him a total of $650,000, per ESPN's Field Yates, and his value resulted in a third-round pick and priceless mentorship.

He appeared to forge an endearing friendship with Mendoza, who eagerly absorbed tips and tricks from Cousins.

Las Vegas drafted Mendoza first overall in the aftermath of his prolific 2025 season with the Hoosiers. He won the Heisman Trophy, vaulted himself into the end zone en route to beating Miami in the national championship and finished the season with 48 total touchdowns, including 41 through the air.

His effervescence, often on full display in postgame interviews, made him a unique college football star. He's still that happy-go-lucky QB, at least outside the white lines.

Time will tell how his game translates to NFL regular-season play. He completed six of his eight passes against the Patriots for 48 yards. In the preseason, he had mixed results, impressing in his debut against the Arizona Cardinals and then throwing a pick-6 versus the Houston Texans and another interception against the San Francisco 49ers.

Mendoza wrapped the preseason, according to Pro Football Focus, with 250 yards on 26-of-46 passing, registering a 56.5% completion rate, one touchdown pass and those two picks.

It's been months since then, however. The Cousins trade speaks to Minnesota's desperation for a quarterback solution, but it also says a lot about the Raiders' trust in Mendoza's development.

#2776. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2774. 6 winners and losers from the Patriots’ trade deadline inactivity

The 2026 NFL trade deadline saw some big moves being made, but the New England Patriots did not join the fun. The team of head coach Mike Vrabel instead decided to let the Tuesday afternoon deadline come and go without either acquiring any players from the outside or moving on from some of their current personnel.

As a consequence, the roster will largely stay intact heading toward a Week 10 matchup with the Detroit Lions in Munich. Who can be seen as the primary benefactors of that inactivity, though? Here are some names that come to mind.

RB Corey Kiner and RB Lan Larison: With Rhamondre Stevenson reportedly set to miss time due to a knee injury, and with TreVeyon Henderson sidelined because of an illness, the Patriots adding some running back depth ahead of the deadline would not have come as too big of a surprise. The Colts' Jonathan Taylor or the Ravens' Derrick Henry were among the names mentioned as potential candidate, but even players with lesser star power would have negatively impacted the current group of backups. However, no trade happening can be seen as a vote of confidence in the likes of Corey Kiner and Lan Larison.

DT Christian Barmore: For starters, Carlton Davis getting traded always felt more like media speculation than anything else, so we are not going to spend much time on him. Christian Barmore, on the hand, could have changed teams had an attractive offer come along. It didn't meaning that he will stay put for the time being. Of course, Barmore's long-term outlook beyond the 2026 is still uncertain: while he can be a disruptive player and is currently ranked fifth on the Patriots with 15 quarterback pressures, he also is primarily a passing-down player that is being paid like a three-down contributor.

ED Harold Landry III, maybe: Pre-deadline rumors mentioned the Patriots as a potential landing spot for an edge rusher to complement a depth chart currently led by Dre'Mont Jones, Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas. No extra players being brought aboard means that the trio will continue leading the charge, but also that New England does feel at least good enough about its depth and positional outlook not to invest any extra resources in bolstering the group. One could interpret this as positive news for one player in particular: Harold Landry, who remains on the PUP list but is a candidate to be reactivated for the Patriots' home stretch. If the team felt uncertain about his ability to return at one point, it might have been more aggressive pursuing depth at the spot.

Depth receivers: A.J. Brown is nearing a return, but his latest absence due to a knee issue showed that the Patriots' wide receiver group is thin especially at the perimeter; Kyle Williams, the next man up, did little with the extended opportunity he received over the last two weeks and during Brown's previous stint on IR with a sprained ankle. Still, no outside help being added is good news for him and fellow depth receiver Efton Chism. The same is true for the depth at tight end, where Cameron Latu remains the de facto TE3 now that New England opted against bolstering his position group.

Receiver depth (and more): Of course, while the Patriots forgoing making any moves is good news for the individual players not negatively affected, it also means that the questions coming out of the Week 9 loss to the Packers remain. Kyle Williams is still the next man up at wide receiver, and Cameron Latu possibly one snap away from meaningful offensive playing time. Likewise, the Patriots' best-case scenario at right guard remains their second-stringer being able to return to the 53-man roster off of injured reserve. They also are putting a lot of trust in those aforementioned Corey Kiner and Lan Larison, the three-player edge rotation, and other positions who could on paper have benefitted from some fresh talent.

Next men up: Christian Barmore not getting traded suggests that the Patriots' status quo at defensive tackle will not change: Barmore is still a top-three guy alongside Milton Williams and Cory Durden. Had he been removed from the mix, the depth options — with Leonard Taylor probably the first name worth mentioning — would have been given more high-quality opportunities in the rotation.

The defensive outlook: Had the Vikings decided not to trade for now-former Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins on Tuesday, the Patriots defense would have looked at its Week 14 matchup with Minnesota as a favorable matchup. Before Cousins joined the mix, Kyler Murray, Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer were the only QBs on the team's roster. Needless to say that Cousins, while not a world-beater himself, is an upgrade over that trio — and more of a challenge for New England's defense when the Vikings come to town in mid-December.

#2772. Koa Peat’s development requires patience amid Suns’ early struggles

You could feel it last night during the loss to the San Antonio Spurs, couldn't you? When Suns' rookie wing Koa Peat entered the game, you could feel that "disease of what if" beginning to creep in. Perhaps I felt it more than most because I'd spent my morning browsing eBay, looking through the newly released 2026-27 Topps basketball cards and hunting for Peat rookie cards. Side note: I love that they're doing the 45th anniversary of the 1981-82 Topps cards. Classically beautiful.

So when he entered the game with 5:56 left and the Suns trailing by 30 points in the fourth quarter, I suddenly had a reason to remain engaged for the rest of the evening. And he didn't disappoint. The first time Peat touched the ball, he attacked the cylinder, drove left, spun right, and banked a beautiful 6-foot shot off the glass for two points. On the very next possession, he found himself in transition and tossed an alley-oop to Michael Jordan reincarnated in Jamaree Bouyea for another two points.

I felt it deep within my soul. We need to get this guy minutes!

Then reality quickly set in. There aren't necessarily minutes available for him right now, and one of the primary reasons those two possessions looked so beautiful was sitting comfortably on the San Antonio bench. Victor Wembanyama, the very villain responsible for putting Phoenix in a 30-point hole, wasn't on the floor to swat either opportunity into the fifth row.

When you're watching a team that desperately lacks size and rebounding, any opportunity to see a player who possesses those attributes immediately feels like you've stumbled upon the solution. You begin convincing yourself that the coaching staff doesn't know what it's doing, that players like Peat should be receiving consistent opportunities because they offer something the current rotation is sorely missing.

On paper, that sounds wonderful. In reality, it's not nearly that simple, and there are legitimate reasons why it shouldn't happen right now.

For starters, where are those minutes supposed to come from? Ryan Dunn has been playing out of his mind to begin the season. Are we supposed to take some of his limited 16.7 minutes away? Do we cut his playing time in half so Peat can get on the floor long enough to work up a sweat without ever establishing enough rhythm to make those minutes meaningful?

Granted, if we could carve out some minutes from Jalen Green, I'd certainly entertain that conversation. Perhaps that's where an opportunity exists. But the reality is that developing chemistry and cohesion requires consistency within your rotations. You can't expect players to become comfortable with one another if you're constantly reshuffling responsibilities and playing time every time a rookie enters a game and strings together two positive possessions.

Quite honestly, if Peat is receiving significant minutes right now, it probably means the Suns have shifted their priorities away from winning in the present and toward developing for the future. As I've stated before, losing doesn't benefit this franchise. Phoenix doesn't control its own draft destiny, so intentionally prioritizing development at the expense of winning creates a situation where you're accumulating losses without receiving the traditional reward that comes with them. You might as well go out there and try to win basketball games.

There will eventually come a time when development becomes a greater priority. If the Suns remain 12th in the Western Conference standings as the season progresses, the organization may need to reevaluate its approach and provide more meaningful opportunities to its younger players. At that point, giving Peat, Fleming, and others additional minutes could become an important part of determining what the future looks like.

But we're nine games into the season. Nine. And while I recognize there are people already pounding their fists on the table demanding more playing time for Peat, I'm here to tell you that now is neither the time nor the place.

That's the challenge of the disease of what if. It sends your mind wandering toward hypothetical solutions that seem perfectly logical when you're watching your team get dismantled. You see a young player make a couple of exciting plays, recognize that he possesses attributes your team desperately needs, and begin imagining how differently things might have unfolded had he been given an opportunity earlier.

But countless variables contribute to those moments. The opponent's personnel, the score, the defensive intensity, the matchups, and the circumstances surrounding those opportunities all matter. And because you'll never receive a definitive answer to what would have happened had that player entered the game earlier, the hypothetical begins to feel like a solution.

Adding some fuel to the debate is that Suns' head coach Jordan Ott stated just a few days ago that Peat is "right on the cusp."

"Koa is next and Koa's right there on the tip," Ott stated. "We understand that he's young and he's hasn't done doesn't have a ton of NBA game experience, but again, the way the game is moving, the ability to drive, process, and defend the drive, he appears to have it, and he's right there. He'll get his opportunity, and we have full faith that that's what's coming."

The Suns could certainly use some help on the glass, as last night's loss served as another painful reminder of how difficult it has been for this team to secure rebounds. Phoenix was outrebounded by 20 against San Antonio and currently ranks dead last in the NBA with a 44.6% overall rebounding percentage. Perhaps even more concerning is its defensive rebounding percentage, which sits at a league-worst 60.1%. That means opposing teams have an alarmingly high likelihood of extending possessions by grabbing offensive rebounds, a recurring nightmare for Phoenix.

The consequences are showing up on the scoreboard. The Suns allow a league-high 19.0 second-chance points per game, essentially handing opponents additional scoring opportunities because they cannot consistently finish defensive possessions with a rebound. It's difficult enough to stop NBA offenses the first time around. When you're giving them multiple opportunities to score on the same possession, you're making an already challenging task nearly impossible.

Where do I land on Koa Peat? I want to see him play. I want to see what he can become, and I certainly want the Suns to develop the talent they've invested in. But wanting to see more of a player and believing he deserves more minutes right now are two different things.

The Suns have to balance the future with the present, and nine games into the season, they still have a responsibility to compete. Maybe Peat eventually earns a larger role. Maybe the circumstances change and create that opportunity. Until then, we have to resist the temptation to turn two exciting possessions into an answer to problems that are considerably more complicated. The disease of what if is powerful, but it doesn't necessarily make the prescription any better.

Me? I'll just head back over to eBay and hunt more rookie autos.

#2769. NHL Rumours: Philadelphia Flyers Forward Seeking Change of Scenery

Things are heating up in Philadelphia. The Philadelphia Flyers, amid their tumultuous start this season, may be facing more internal turmoil. Matvei Michkov has made it clear over the last week that he has been unhappy with his ice time with the Flyers. It should come as no surprise that NHL Rumours regarding the Flyers' leading goal scorer have surfaced.

Rumour: According to NHL analyst Kevin Weekes, Philadelphia Flyers forward Matvei Michkov is open to a change of scenery. Over the past week, Michkov has expressed discontent over his ice time, as Head Coach Rick Tocchet and Michkov have continued to have a difficult relationship. However, according to Emily Kaplan, Michkov has not formally requested a trade.

Analysis: This is a very intriguing rumour, as it expands the trade market, with the Dylan Larkin trade rumours and Nikita Kucherov trade request still active. Given that Michkov is wanting more ice time, this would be the best possible option for him.

To start this edition of NHL Rumours, let us go over Michkov's time with the Flyers. Over the past week, Michkov has talked to the media about his ice time."I want to play more," commented Michkov. "I like it all maximum, all shifts, all ice time, I want 60 minutes. Michkov's time with the Flyers has been a roller coaster. The seventh-overall pick in 2023 was seen by some as potentially the most talented player after Connor Bedard in his draft class. His contract with the KHL was a reason why some teams passed on him. However, Michkov was able to negotiate to be released from the KHL and joined Philadelphia for the 2024-25 season. His offensive production was prominent right away, as he scored 26 goals and 63 points in 80 games during his rookie year.

The defensive aspect of his game was a concern, but it was not until Rick Tocchet was hired that the problems started to surface. Michkov came to training camp out of shape, according to Tocchet. For Vancouver Canucks fans, this may sound eerily similar to how he dealt with Elias Pettersson, whose production also dipped during Tocchet's tenure. Sure, there may be truth to Tocchet's statements, but no doubt, it must have been frustrating from Michkov's perspective to see a reduction in ice time.

Michkov showed an improvement in his offseason preparation this season, but the team did not. Although Michkov's production has been solid, his ice time remains low, as Tocchet's deployment of young players remains a concern among both Michkov himself and the fans, who have voiced their displeasure over the deployment of young players through a fundraiser over the weekend. The fundraiser is looking to fund a banner reading "Fire Tocchet" that would fly over Xfinity Mobile Arena on November 27th, alongside a billboard near the arena.

Last night against the Vancouver Canucks, Michkov had a heated conversation with Nick Seeler over what could be Seeler's poor play. Porter Martone and Noel Acciari had to hold him back as Michkov's rage led him to throw a water bottle. Michkov's frustrations may have boiled over, because not only is he not getting the ice time he feels he deserves, but the team was also not playing the right way against the last-place Canucks.

It is clear that Michkov does not feel appreciated in Philadelphia, and a future with the team does not feel tenable. Given his offensive talent, many teams will be interested in the 21-year-old forward. No doubt, teams will be careful with Michkov's defensive inadequacies, but the offensive upside is still too good to pass up. Michkov is in the final season of his three-year entry-level contract and will be eligible for an offer sheet, so whichever team ends up taking Michkov will need to act relatively quickly in signing him to an extension.

#2765. LeBron Log No. 4: A courtside sip, 16,000 makes and Cleveland's welcome

LeBron Log No. 4: A courtside sip, 16,000 makes and Cleveland's welcome originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James' latest week with the Sixers included a sip of a stranger's wine, yet another number no NBA player had reached and a return to the city where his career began.

It also included his worst performance with Philadelphia, followed less than 48 hours later by his highest-scoring game with the team.

Welcome to the fourth edition of the LeBron Log.

No chronicle of James' first season in Philadelphia could omit the time he helped himself to a fan's wine during a game.

James chased Tyrese Maxey's transition pass into the stands during the third quarter of the Sixers' Nov. 2 win over the Bulls. He collided with Philadelphia native Troy Clemons, spilled some of Clemons' wine and sampled what had landed on his arm.

The interaction received its own story on our site, and deservedly so. It also belongs in the Log.

Clemons did not keep the cup as a souvenir. He threw it away and got another drink.

James returned to the court and later broke into a dance after scoring over the 6-foot-1 Tre Jones. The wine clip generated millions of views across social media and became the defining image from an otherwise ordinary 19-point Sixers victory.

The following night in Detroit, James offered a broader explanation for why Philadelphia has already looked comfortable together.

"We've got a good team," James said. "Guys vibe with one another. Guys like each other. Guys enjoy being around each other. That has a lot to do with it, too. It makes the game a lot easier when you enjoy being around people."

Eleven games into his Sixers career, James appears to be doing exactly that.

James arrived in Detroit two baskets away from another unprecedented number.

His second field goal against the Pistons made him the first player in NBA history to reach 16,000 regular-season field goals.

James finished the Sixers' 112-106 victory with 13 points, 10 rebounds and eight assists. The near-triple-double helped Philadelphia improve to 8-1 and avenge its only loss of the season.

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar ranks second in league history with 15,837 made field goals. Karl Malone is a distant third at 13,528. James is the only active player with more than 12,000.

His scoring record has long been secure. James passed Abdul-Jabbar in career points in February 2023 and later overtook him in made baskets. The round number in Detroit still illustrated the distance he has created between himself and every other scorer.

James began his career by making 5,361 field goals across seven seasons with Cleveland. He added 3,510 in Miami, returned to make 3,691 more for the Cavaliers and made another 3,421 during eight years with the Lakers.

Basket No. 16,000 belonged to Philadelphia.

The Sixers' 8-1 start also carried a notable James connection. Each of his previous four teams to begin a season at least 7-1 reached the NBA Finals.

James was not ready to entertain that conversation in early November.

"It's too early to be talking about the Finals and things of that nature," he said. "We've got to continue to buy into what we want to do."

Two nights later, James returned to the place where nearly half of those 16,000 baskets were made.

His first game in Cleveland as a Sixer brought out jerseys from every stop of his career. Cavaliers colors filled Rocket Arena alongside Heat black, Lakers purple and the Sixers' throwback look.

James received a warm ovation when he was introduced last among Philadelphia's starters. When he checked out late in the fourth quarter, with the result decided, the crowd stood for him again.

James has experienced both ends of Cleveland's emotional range.

He returned as a member of the Heat on Dec. 2, 2010, to one of the most hostile receptions in NBA history. Six years later, he delivered the Cavaliers their first championship and ended Cleveland's 52-year major professional sports title drought.

"I've seen the depths of hell when it comes to a reception here, all the way to the heavens above," James said. "Anything in between is easy money."

The reception fell somewhere in the middle. His performance landed much closer to the bottom.

James finished with eight points on 3-for-12 shooting, three assists and six turnovers in the Sixers' 119-95 loss. It was his first single-digit performance in Cleveland since he scored three points against the Rockets on Dec. 30, 2004.

He had scored at least 10 points in 396 consecutive regular-season games in the city. The run covered his first stint with the Cavaliers, every visit as an opponent and his entire second tenure with the organization.

It ended during his first trip back in a Sixers uniform.

"I definitely did not feel in a good rhythm offensively," James said. "A couple of them were careless. A couple of them were just trying to make the right play and not being successful with it."

It was only the 10th single-digit regular-season game of James' 1,630-game career. He still took time afterward to consider what an eventual jersey retirement in Cleveland could represent.

"The journey from being an 18-year-old rookie, to leading a franchise to a championship," James said. "And everything in between."

James did not carry the rough night into Chicago.

Less than 48 hours after struggling in Cleveland, he scored a season-high 22 points in the Sixers' 127-121 victory over the Bulls. Thirteen came during the second quarter, when James helped Philadelphia turn an early deficit into a halftime lead.

His first basket produced another milestone.

James entered Sunday trailing Abdul-Jabbar's 1,895 points for the most scored against the Bulls in NBA history. His first-quarter three-pointer moved him into the lead. He ended the afternoon with 1,916.

The most interesting play from his night was a pass.

With the Sixers ahead by four and 2:20 remaining, James drove into the paint. Three Chicago defenders collapsed toward him. Maxey stood between the left wing and corner, but even he did not believe James could see him.

James fired the ball through the defense. Maxey sidestepped Isaac Okoro and made the three-pointer, pushing Philadelphia's lead to seven.

After his postgame interview, James pulled out his phone and watched the play again.

"He didn't think I saw him," James called out from his locker as reporters asked Maxey about the possession.

Maxey acknowledged that he had positioned himself to rebound because he expected James to shoot.

"Honestly, I was like this," Maxey said, raising his hands. "I thought he was about to shoot a layup."

James has spent the opening weeks of the season teaching his new teammates to expect the unexpected pass.

"You've got to become a wide receiver or a catcher at that point," Maxey said. "You never know when you're going to get the ball.

#2761. Kirk Cousins can become the first quarterback to play an 18-game regular season

With the Raiders trading him to the Vikings, Kirk Cousins has an opportunity to do something no quarterback has done before: Play 18 games in a single regular season.

Cousins has already started nine games this season for the Raiders, who have not had their bye. He’s now joining the Vikings, who have nine games left on their schedule because they have already had their bye. If Cousins plays every game the rest of the season, he’ll have played 18 regular-season games.

Since the NFL expanded the regular season to 17 games over 18 weeks in 2021, four players have played 18 games in a regular season because they moved from a team that hadn’t had its bye to a team that had: Rashid Shaheed and Dre’Mont Jones in 2025, Mike Williams in 2024 and Leonard Williams in 2023.

The NFL record for games in a season is actually 19, set by four members of the Frankford Yellow Jackets, a team that routinely played more games than other NFL teams in the 1920s. But in the modern era, 18 games has been the most a player could conceivably pay, and Cousins, as a starting quarterback, may become the most noteworthy player to do it.

#2758. Observations after well-balanced Sixers hold off Bulls

Observations after well-balanced Sixers hold off Bulls originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Still no losing streaks to speak of for the 2026-27 Sixers.

The Sixers earned a 127-121 win Sunday over the Bulls to wrap up a 2-1 road trip. They moved to 9-2 overall and Chicago fell to 1-8.

Every Sixers starter scored in double figures.

Three reached the 20-point mark in Jaylen Brown (29 points), Tyrese Maxey (27 points) and LeBron James (22). Joel Embiid had 18 points and 10 rebounds.

Josh Giddey posted 19 points, 15 assists and seven rebounds for the Bulls.

The Sixers were without Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain), Dominick Barlow (lower back stress reaction) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear). The Bulls' absences included Norman Powell (right shoulder inflammation/soreness) and Zach Collins (respiratory illness).

Next on the Sixers' schedule is a home game Tuesday night vs. the Celtics. Here are observations on their win over Chicago:

Following his 0-for-9 night Friday in the Sixers' loss to the Cavaliers, Embiid did not snap right back into form.

He was well short on his first shot attempt, a wide-open three-pointer. Embiid then failed to score in the post over Jalen Smith.

Embiid got a field goal to go at the 6:42 mark of the first quarter when he tipped in his own miss. However, Smith canned a three on the ensuing possession to give Chicago a 23-16 lead.

James committed two early turnovers, although he did sink a corner three-pointer during a fast-paced first quarter. VJ Edgecombe added two long-range jumpers in the first.

Entering Sunday, the Sixers' minus-9.6 net rating in the first quarter ranked 27th in the NBA. They managed to hold a one-point lead in Chicago after the first.

The Sixers' offensive rebounding was their greatest strength in the first quarter. They poured in 17 second-chance points. Embiid had four offensive boards in the opening frame.

Jabari Walker assumed backup center duties for the second straight game without Bona. He picked up where Embiid left off on the glass, grabbing seven rebounds (three offensive) in a great first stint.

Though he's undersized in the height department for an NBA center at 6-foot-7, Walker has plenty of rebounding tools.

He's listed at a strong 237 pounds, doesn't mind contact whatsoever, hunts the ball, and has a knack for winning contested boards. Walker showed all of that Sunday. Very hard to overstate how well he rebounded.

The Sixers' first-shot offense also had many bright moments in the second quarter.

James got rolling on his way to a 16-point first half, Embiid made a couple of mid-range jumpers, and Maxey hit two free throws put the Sixers up 60-50 late in the second period.

Chicago evened the game at 68-all early in the third quarter on a Matas Buzelis three, but the Bulls couldn't sustain that run.

The Bulls' defense continued to look like one of the worst in the NBA and the Sixers' well-balanced offense kept the scoreboard moving. Brown nailed a turnaround jumper to give his team a double-digit lead. Walker knocked down a top-of-the-key triple to extend the Sixers' advantage to 12 points.

The Sixers had two apparent injury scares in the second half. Brown limped to the sideline with 6:55 to go in the third quarter, but he stayed in the game. Edgecombe headed to the locker room after subbing out at the 9:08 mark of the fourth quarter. He returned to the Sixers' bench and ultimately returned for a final stint.

On the floor, the Sixers couldn't ease to victory. Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson trimmed Chicago's deficit to 116-113 by draining a three. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse called timeout.

The Sixers were efficient enough in the half court down the stretch.

Embiid made a put-back hoop and a pair of free throws. Maxey drilled a side-step three-ball after a wraparound feed from James. The Sixers converted their clutch free throws and secured a winning road trip.

#2757. With NFL's toughest schedule looming, Rams quiet at trade deadline as rivals make deals

High-profile trades before the season showed their fans and the rest of the NFL that with Super Bowl LXI to be played at SoFi Stadium, the Rams were unquestionably all in.

But as the league's trade deadline came and went Tuesday, the injury-ravaged Rams made only one minor move, essentially saying they'll handle this all internally.

While the NFC West-leading San Francisco 49ers added veteran receiver Keenan Allen, the Rams — with Davante Adams on injured reserve and Puka Nacua expected to be sidelined for an extended period — brought back receiver Xavier Smith, whom they released in October.

Read more: Rams star Puka Nacua likely will be placed on injured reserve

That is a far cry from moves the Rams made in previous Super Bowl seasons. In 2018, they traded for edge rusher Dante Fowler Jr. In 2021, they signed free-agent receiver Odell Beckham Jr. and traded for edge rusher Von Miller.

Coach Sean McVay indicated the last few weeks that the Rams were unlikely to be active at the deadline.

But that was before last Sunday, when Nacua suffered knee and toe injuries that are expected to sideline the All-Pro receiver for several weeks. The Rams were already thin at receiver after Adams suffered a hamstring injury that has kept him out of the lineup since Week 7.

"You have to look at all avenues to try to be able to solve some of the issues or situations or scenarios that have come up," McVay said Monday when asked if the Rams might pursue a receiver. "A lot of new things occur on a daily basis, so I would never rule it out."

Allen and Josh Downs of the Indianapolis Colts and Brian Thomas Jr. of the Jacksonville Jaguars were thought to be potential targets for the Rams.

Rams general manager Les Snead. (Kyusung Gong / Associated Press)

But the Jaguars ultimately took Thomas off the market. The 49ers, with receiver depth problems of their own, added Allen, and the Kansas City Chiefs traded for Downs.

The 49ers' move came after they had traded for defensive lineman DeForest Buckner ahead of the deadline. And the defending Super Bowl-champion Seattle Seahawks had bolstered their roster by trading for All-Pro offensive lineman Quenton Nelson.

Barring the Rams signing a free agent — the Minnesota Vikings released Beckham after the deadline and signed him to their practice squad — they will go into Sunday's game against the Arizona Cardinals with a receiver corps that includes Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell, rookie CJ Daniels and Smith. The Rams re-signed Smith from the 49ers' practice squad after placing Jordan Whittington on injured reserve.

The Rams are 5-4 and have won three games in a row. But according to ESPN, they have the league's toughest remaining schedule.

Read more: 'I am that closer.' Myles Garrett's three-sack performance shows why Rams traded for him

After playing at the Cardinals, the Rams will have what is essentially a mini-bye before playing the Green Bay Packers at SoFi Stadium on the night before Thanksgiving.

Then they play the Chiefs, at the 49ers, the Dallas Cowboys and games against the Seahawks sandwiched around a game at Tampa Bay.

Defensive lineman Kobie Turner is expected to return against the Packers, and Adams, Nacua, tight end Terrance Ferguson and offensive lineman Steve Avila will be available at some point. But whether the Rams can remain in contention for a playoff spot is the all-encompassing question.

#2756. 5 things Packers must do to win Super Bowl after quiet trade deadline

The trade deadline has come and gone without the Green Bay Packers making a significant move to upgrade the team, meaning their roster is pretty much set in stone for the rest of the season.

It was no surprise to see Brian Gutekunst stand pat, as there were very few options that actually made sense for Green Bay, especially if looking only at the players who were actually traded somewhere.

They were obviously not in a position to make big swings like the Bears and Jaguars did for Jeffery Simmons or Jordan Davis at defensive tackle, respectively, due to the hefty draft capital involved. DeForest Buckner could have been an option, but he only wanted to go to the 49ers.

Adding Quenton Nelson to the offensive line would have been nice. He was not cheap though and is a left guard only, with the right side more of the issue right now. Running backs Jonathan Taylor and Tony Pollard ended up not getting moved.

The Packers already made multiple signings on the offensive line in-season and Kevin Zeitler only saw his first snaps on Sunday. It is fair to let that situation play itself out as Green Bay keeps trying to figure out their 'best five' (more on that shortly).

With the roster unlikely to change much from here on out, and fresh off a dominant win in New England, here is what needs to happen for a Packers team that now looks like a real contender to win the Super Bowl:

Green Bay has already had its fill of devastating injuries to important players this season, with Zach Bako-Bewele, Jayden Reed, Edgerrin Cooper and Javon Hargrave all done for the year.

There are still eight regular seasons to go, and more injuries are bound to happen. The Packers cannot afford for any more of the season-ending variety to the caliber of players that have already been lost.

Jordan Love is 1A on that list, and this exceptionally explosive passing attack would also not be the same without either Christian Watson or Matthew Golden.

Tucker Kraft and arguably Jordan Morgan – who has really locked down the left side in pass protection lately – are also indispensable on offense given the lack of options behind them.

On defense, Jonathan Gannon has overcome some big losses, as well as the absence of Micah Parsons without skipping a beat, but there is only so much the group can take before the dam breaks.

They really only have two reliable three-down starters at defensive tackle in Devonte Wyatt and Karl Brooks, although they will hope to get Warren Brinson back from IR at some point.

The real engine of this defense is the secondary though, and if one of the tremendous trio of Evan Williams, Xavier McKinney or Javon Bullard went down, the knock-on effect on the entire unit could be massive.

Green Bay needs to pray to the injury gods that there are no more crushing blows on the horizon if this team is to go on a serious run.

More specifically, play Zeitler at right guard and Laken Tomlinson at left guard. PFF is certainly not gospel, but they gave Zeitler a 73.9 grade in his debut against the Patriots (in admittedly only 20 snaps), while Tomlinson has a 68.1 grade for the season.

Aaron Banks, who is still getting the red carpet treatment despite constantly being injured and not performing when he is in the lineup, has a 39.1 grade on the year.

The persistence with Banks, even forcing Tomlinson out of position to right guard to accommodate him, is likely due to his massive paycheck, and frankly that is not a good enough reason. It needs to stop, and it does seem like the tide is turning after Sunday's game.

Get Zeitler into the lineup, keep both him and Tomlinson at their natural spots and let the offensive line build chemistry. Once Sean Rhyan returns from injury, they may have a legitimately serviceable offensive line, which looked like a pipe dream two months ago.

There were also some green shoots in the run game against New England, as Green Bay managed four yards per carry as a team (the previous average was a paltry 2.85) and Kaleb Johnson had an encouraging day with a 4.9-yard average.

The Patriots are not usually easy to run against, and while the constant threat of the ball being thrown over their heads probably helped, that is an absolutely fine formula for the Packers to lean on moving forward, using the pass to set up the run, rather than the other way around.

If Green Bay can form some semblance of a viable run game by the time the playoffs arrive, centered around Johnson, Josh Jacobs and Karl Brooks, it will be a game changer for what has looked like one of the worst rushing attacks of all time for much of the year.

The wait to see Parsons back on the field has been longer than expected, so hopefully it will be worth it when he finally does suit up, which may come on Thanksgiving eve against the Rams.

Gannon has done a remarkable job with the defense, fashioning it into one of the league's best. A fit and firing Parsons could take them to a nuclear level.

While it will surely take him some time to get his feet back under him and look like his old self, Parsons needs to be at full power by the postseason to turn this into a true championship defense.

Sunday was a massive step forward for Smack after some real struggles of late. Relying on a rookie kicker is scary, as it can seem like they are rounding into form at times, before suffering another setback. Progression is not always linear.

That is the cost of doing business, but it can also cost you playoff games, as the Packers found out with Anders Carlson a few years back. By season's end, Green Bay must be in a position where they are able to trust Smack to deliver when it matters.

#2755. Chargers trade Daiyan Henley to Broncos for 2027 fourth, 2028 fifth-round picks

The last-place team in the AFC West is trading a player to the first-place team in the AFC West.

The Chargers have traded linebacker Daiyan Henley to the Broncos for a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick.

For the Broncos, it’s an addition of a linebacker who has started every game but one for the Chargers over the last three seasons, and should be able to step in and contribute immediately in Denver.

For the Chargers, it’s an addition of two draft picks for a winless team that desperately needs to build for the future. Henley is in the final season of his rookie contract as a 2023 third-round pick and might have left the Chargers this offseason anyway. Now the Chargers are getting something for him.

Henley is a defensive captain, and there were reports that the Chargers weren’t looking to trade important players, but realistically, when you’re the worst team in the league, you’re going to trade players for picks if a good offer comes your way.

Some teams prefer not to trade with division rivals, but in this case, it’s a trade that should benefit both teams, so there’s no reason for both teams not to do it. And now Henley will attempt to win the AFC West this season, something he was not going to do in Los Angeles.
