#2752. NY Giants trade deadline analysis: Nothing happened, and that’s OK

The New York Giants tried to make a splash at the NFL trade deadline. They ended up not able to do anything.

Running back Jonathan Taylor was, of course, the player the Giants had targeted as a difference-maker for their offense — for this season and at least a couple of years to come. The Indianapolis Colts, though, chose to set a price tag no one, including the Giants, was willing to meet.

Multiple teams offered a second-round pick and more for Taylor. But the Colts wanted a blockbuster offer to even consider it. Instead, Taylor stays in Indy.

Giants head coach John Harbaugh said an hour before the deadline that he would be excited to have the "right player" join the team as it tries to win its first NFC East title since 2011.

"My excitement level would be based on who the player is," Harbaugh said. "You get the right player, then you're really excited."

Taylor could have been that guy. The price, though, was wrong.

"You don't want to make a bad deal. You make a bad deal, that doesn't make you better. That makes you worse," Harbaugh said. "Sometimes the best deal is a deal that you don't make.

"We're willing to pay a price to make our team better, but it's got to be something that really makes our team better, and it's got to be worth it."

On Monday, I asked Harbaugh about the idea of trying not to make an emotional decision at the trade deadline with the excitement of defeating the Philadelphia Eagles and leading the division being fresh.

Harbaugh said it was "very important" to take the emotion of the moment out of the decision-making process.

"You want to do everything you can do to make your team as strong as you can right now, because we're in the now, and we're told to live in the moment, be where our feet are planted, concern ourselves with today, but that's not at the expense of tomorrow or just prudent planning," Harbaugh said. "I think we just have to look at each situation, and just weigh it out in terms of, okay, what's the cost? What's the benefit? And is it worth it? Is it going to benefit us? Is it a good thing for the Giants, and for the organization, and the team?"

Taylor would have made the Giants stronger right now. The Giants, though, were correct to not overpay for a 27-year-old running back with high mileage. Just like they were correct a couple of years ago when they did not overpay in free agency for a 27-year-old running back with high mileage.

In the days leading up to the deadline, we watched the Jacksonville Jaguars make multiple trades — including outrageously giving the Philadelphia Eagles first- and second-round picks for defensive tackle Jordan Davis. We saw the Minnesota Vikings trade for quarterback Kirk Cousins. We saw the Buffalo Bills, San Francisco 49ers, and Kansas City Chiefs make "now" trades.

All of those teams have designs on winning a Super Bowl this season.

The Giants? They are not there yet. Winning the NFC East would be a massive accomplishment. Remember, they won seven games combined the last two seasons. It would be a tremendous step in the right direction for a proud franchise that has been down for most of the last 15 years.

I went on record a few days ago saying that I thought the Giants should make another run at Taylor, but that the price couldn't be more than the second-round pick plus that they had already offered.

Not giving away their first-round pick was the proper decision. In Harbaugh's words, the prudent one.

The Tennessee Titans did not want to trade running back Tony Pollard. He is a nice player, but Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy are nice players, too.

The Giants could have used defensive tackle help. They were never getting Jeffery Simmons, and they weren't foolish enough to give up a first-round pick for Davis. The Colts apparently wanted a fourth-round pick for Grover Stewart. The Giants didn't have one to give. They do have Malachi Fields. They didn't have a fifth-round pick. They do have J.J. McCarthy.

Harbaugh had warned on Sunday that the Giants would protect their future.

"We're not just going to go for a short term fix at an exorbitant cost," he said. "We're not going to do that. That's not where we're at."

Where they are at is leading the NFC East by 2.5 games. They have a 68.9% chance of winning the division, moves or no moves.

Getting Taylor, or another big-time difference-maker at the deadline would have been nice.

In the end, though, I think fans should be happy that Harbaugh and GM Joe Schoen kep their wits about them and protected the future.

The deadline end up to be boring for the Giants. Disappointing even, if you want to call it that. But, the Giants acted properly rather than desperately.

#2751. Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup

Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers couldn't rekindle the magic of their comeback home-opening win over the Cavaliers.

They fell Friday night in NBA Cup action, suffering a 119-95 defeat in Cleveland. The Sixers dipped to 8-2 and the Cavs improved to 5-4.

The Sixers' top scorers were Jaylen Brown (20 points), VJ Edgecombe (19 points) and Tyrese Maxey (17).

The Cavs got 23 points from Donovan Mitchell and 22 from Evan Mobley.

The Sixers' injured players included center Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain). Cleveland was down big man Jarrett Allen (right knee contusion). Sam Merrill sat out the second half with a right elbow injury.

With Friday's loss, the Sixers are 1-1 in Eastern Conference Group B of the NBA Cup. Their next Cup game is scheduled for Nov. 25 against the Heat.

The Sixers will conclude their three-road trip Sunday afternoon against the Bulls. Here are observations on their blowout loss to Cleveland:

After a missed Merrill three-pointer, the Sixers steamed ahead on the fast break and Edgecombe opened the scoring with a slam.

The Cavs replied with a 15-0 run kickstarted by six straight Mitchell points. Much like in the Sixers' Oct. 22 win over Cleveland, they were many levels below their best in the first quarter.

The Sixers began 0 for 4 from three-point range, including two LeBron James misses. The Cavs were also the better team in transition and limited the Sixers' chances to attack in the open floor by taking excellent care of the ball in the early going. Edgecombe was called for his second foul with 7:34 left in the first quarter.

Meanwhile, Joel Embiid expressed his frustration about a couple of early no-calls. Embiid's larger problem was that he couldn't hit any sort of shot besides free throws.

He went 0 for 9 from the floor in the game. The seven-time All-Star finished with six points and seven rebounds.

Embiid has had a subpar shooting start to the year, especially from three-point territory — he's now 3 for 28 (10.7 percent) — but Friday was the kind of extreme night that's bound to happen here and there over the course of a long season.

Of course, it's notable that Embiid's been playing through right foot plantar fasciitis and the Sixers have been keeping a close eye on his minutes. We'll see how the team manages his availability moving forward and whether Embiid is able to bounce back next time out.

James didn't play anywhere near his finest game either. He had eight points on 3-for-12 shooting, eight rebounds, three assists and six turnovers.

As a team, the Sixers were 36.5 percent from the field and 25 percent beyond the arc.

Jabari Walker rejoined the Sixers' rotation as the backup center with Bona sidelined. Anfernee Simons, former Cav Dean Wade and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope all remained rotation fixtures.

With Walker and Caldwell-Pope on the court next to three starters, the Sixers cut their deficit to single digits in the second quarter. Walker threw down a fast-break dunk that cut Cleveland's lead to 48-41. He gave the Sixers some good defensive possessions when switched on to James Harden and provided his usual physical, high-effort work on the glass.

Edgecombe was fantastic in the second, sinking three triples, racking up 15 points and nabbing three steals.

Many second-year players would have a tough time finding a rhythm after encountering early foul trouble, but Edgecombe was great as soon as he checked back in and delivered a ton of valuable buckets in the Sixers' comeback push.

The Sixers pulled to within 66-63 when Maxey picked a steal and threw a pretty one-handed bounce pass to Edgecombe for a dunk.

With Embiid and James offering little as scorers, Brown hit several shots that helped the Sixers stay in the game. After his 30-point performance last time out against the Pistons, Brown reached the 20-point mark for a third consecutive game.

Still, the Sixers' offense never got rolling. The Cavs maintained their lead and extended it late in the third quarter. By early in the fourth, the Sixers trailed by over 20 points.

Embiid didn't play the fourth quarter and logged 25 minutes. He's had zero made field goals on just one other occasion in his career, back in Nov. 2019 against the Raptors.

Even with their tremendous first nine games, the Sixers knew they'd hit speed bumps throughout the year. They'll try to get back on track Sunday in Chicago.

CINCINNATI (AP) — The Cincinnati Bengals backed out of a trade for Philadelphia Eagles edge rusher Arnold Ebiketie because it would have resulted in the loss of a third-round compensatory pick in the 2027 NFL draft.

#2748. The Kirk Cousins contract points to a revised deal or termination after 2026

The last time the Vikings brought back a key former player for a third-round pick, the reunion didn’t last long. This time, it will last longer — but possibly not beyond the current season.

In 2010, the Vikings sent a third-round pick to the Patriots for receiver Randy Moss, whom the Vikings had traded to the Raiders in 2005. Former coach Brad Childress, calling Moss a “programmatic non-fit,” released Moss after four games.

Now, quarterback Kirk Cousins returns for a third-round pick, and a contract that covers nine regular-season games. His deal with the Raiders was structured to maximize the amount the Falcons owed Cousins for 2026 ($8.7 million, on top of the $90 million he made in 2024 and 2025) with another $10 million paid by the Raiders to Cousins in 2027, in the form of a guaranteed roster bonus not subject to offset.

The contract also includes a 2028 base salary of $78.655 million that becomes fully guaranteed on the fifth day of the 2027 league year. Coupled with a $1.345 million base salary in 2027 that becomes fully guaranteed that same day, the Vikings would be on the hook for $80 million over two years if he’s not released by then.

Without a revised deal, the current contract surely would be torn up by March. The question is whether the Vikings and Cousins would be able to come up with a new contract to replace it.

Much of that depends on how the rest of the year goes. Still, Cousins has the ability to force his way to free agency, for the fourth time in his career, by simply declining to re-do the existing deal.

However it plays out, Cousins can be counted on to make a good business decision. He has $333 million in career earnings, which has him at fourth on the all-time list.

On-field success is a different story. He has made it to the postseason three times in his career, with one playoff win.

If, as expected, the return of Cousins provides a B-12 shot to the Minnesota franchise, he has a realistic chance of getting back to the playoffs. And of winning a second postseason game.

And maybe a third. Hell, maybe even a fourth.

After Minnesota watched Carson Wentz flounder and realized Kyler Murray wouldn't be the answer, a bold move was needed at QB. Paul George's presence back in town was one of the many swirling morning storylines at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

For good reason, former Celtics teammates Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum will draw immense attention Tuesday night. After all, Brown has said there "might be a little lamb chops with some gravy" between the two, if not a full-blown beef.

George told reporters before the Celtics' shootaround that it feels like "a regular game."

"Had I been here eight, nine, 10 years, different story," he said. "I was here two years. Obviously, we didn't have the best of luck or had a great, I think, partnership in terms of my ability to stay healthy and on the floor. So that kind of played into a lot of it.

The 36-year-old George indeed had trouble staying available for sustained stretches as a Sixer. He dealt with a variety of injuries and served a 25-game suspension last season for violating the NBA's anti-drug policy.

George did play well on both ends of the floor for much of the 2026 playoffs. He helped the Sixers come back to win a seven-game first-round series against the Celtics in historic fashion. The nine-time All-Star also brought a veteran steadiness to the Sixers' locker room and was glad to mentor younger players like VJ Edgecombe.

"Just his routine … even when he got hot, he didn't try to force it," Jabari Walker said Tuesday morning. "His game was smooth and I think that's how he is as a person, just not forcing anything and having a calm energy."

George has certainly enjoyed his early days as a Celtic.

Through nine games, he's averaged 20.4 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 2.3 steals while shooting 42.5 percent from three-point range. Boston will enter Tuesday night's matchup second in the Eastern Conference standings at 8-2, the Sixers first at 9-2.

"I've been kind of blown away," George said. "I think it exceeded my expectations since being in Boston. You never know how much culture is involved and how much culture changes your outlook on things and the effect it has mentally, physically, just being in an environment … and the culture that Boston presents.

"So I've been thrilled. I've been playing some of my best basketball of late, and just been enjoying grinding it out with these guys out here. It's a fun style of play and I can't talk (enough) about just the thrill, the happiness and the excitement and joy that it has brought being here."

He was asked what sort of reception he expects from Sixers fans.

"Not sure," George said. "In some ways, I helped land them a future piece for them. So with that, not sure how the reception would be."

#2745. Tale of the tape: Bills were able to find solutions to Vikings blitz as game progressed

The Buffalo Bills learned firsthand that more blockers doesn't guarantee better protection.

The Minnesota Vikings defense entered the game blitzing an NFL-high 71% of the time, more than double the league average. And the Bills came out with a game plan that respected the blitz and the chaos it created.

Throughout much of the first half, the NFL's top-ranked scoring defense outdueled the league's top scoring offense. A combination of miscommunication on the offensive line — which was without left tackle Dion Dawkins (rib) and left guard Alec Anderson (ankle) — a glitch in the game plan and quarterback Josh Allen playing hurriedly caused the passing game to sputter.

But the Bills gradually started to find a rhythm and produced a big scoring drive that ended with an Allen-to-Keleki Latu 25-yard touchdown pass before halftime in a 23-6 win.

Allen went 6 of 11 for 44 yards, an interception and three sacks against the Minnesota blitz during the first half, but turned it around in the second half to go 6 of 9 for 64 yards and a sack when the Vikings sent five or more rushers.

One way the Bills sparked their passing game was by stepping away from heavy protection schemes. Having more blockers may seem like a grand idea to protect Allen, but it actually was what the Vikings wanted them to do.

Minnesota tricks opponents into locking in their protection rules before sending unblocked pressure from unexpected angles. Even if there are more blockers than rushers, it's hard to shift once the protection is set.

And if the offense commits six (or more) blockers for five rushers, the Vikings have more defenders than the offense has receivers in the pattern. Bills coach Joe Brady only sent five receivers out 10 times in the game against the blitz, but they were effective.

With six or more blockers, Allen went 4 of 12 for 40 yards, with an interception and two sacks. On plays with just five blockers, Allen went 8 of 8 for 71 yards and two sacks.

On first down from their own 15-yard line in the second quarter, the Bills tried to run a play-action pass. The protection was faulty, as a miscommunication between left guard Austin Corbett and left tackle Tylan Grable allowed Minnesota defensive tackle Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins to split them.

But the bigger problem was that the Bills only had two receivers in the pattern — both beyond the sticks — and the Vikings had five in coverage. Had a check-down or underneath option been available, Allen could have released the ball quickly to avoid being sacked.

"I don't think we were (efficient on first down) in the first half," Allen said. "In the second half, I thought we wore down on them and skipped some third downs. … Second and long, they're getting to their third down menu, they're making it really tough for opposing offenses. The best way out of that is stay out of second-and-long, third-and-long situations."

With 4:04 left in the third quarter, the Bills got a first down at their own 39 and once again went with a play-action pass. The Vikings only sent five, but the Bills only used five to block them.

The protection was more in sync, with a nifty wrinkle that saw Corbett pull to the right edge and block outside linebacker Kyle Van Noy. And while the Vikings still had a one-man advantage in the secondary, spacing gave Allen multiple options.

Allen could have hit D.J. Moore in the right flat or Ray Davis in the left flat. He also had tight end Dawson Knox over the middle. Throws to Moore and Knox likely would have netted a first down, but Allen also had Khalil Shakir running open 10 yards behind Knox and he delivered it for an easy 22-yard gain.

In a clash between high-powered offense and elite defense, patience ultimately determined the winner — and the Bills outlasted Minnesota.

#2743. Seahawks 2026 trade deadline recap: Seattle doesn’t make any more moves

After the acquisition of All-Pro offensive guard Quenton Nelson on Oct. 27 seemingly made the Seattle Seahawks' intentions clear, general manager John Schneider didn't have the deadline many were expecting.

The Seahawks made no additional moves on Tuesday, despite several reports they were actively exploring the trade market. Including projected compensatory picks, Seattle has 10 selections in the 2027 draft, so the lack of movement was unlikely due to a shortage of assets.

Jaylen Brown was asked Sunday whether he and Jayson Tatum had spoken since the former teammates addressed their relationship during the preseason.

Does he plan to approach Tatum before Tuesday night's game at Xfinity Mobile Arena?

"I mean, he's on his side, I'm on my side," Brown said. "We're playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win. So it's nothing to talk about. Let's check the ball up."

After months of public comments, documentaries and questions about how their partnership ended, the basketball will finally take over.

Brown will face Boston for the first time since the Celtics traded him to Philadelphia for Paul George and four future draft assets in July. He spent his first 10 NBA seasons in Boston, played nine alongside Tatum and helped the Celtics win the 2024 championship, earning Finals MVP honors.

Tuesday's 8 p.m. game on NBC will also bring together the top two teams in the Eastern Conference. The Sixers are 9-2. Boston, riding a three-game winning streak, is 8-2 and sits a half-game behind Philadelphia.

"Another good opportunity for our team to be able to show what we're made of," Brown said. "I'm looking forward to it. Big-time matchup, two heavyweights in the East. Let's get it."

Brown has not hidden his appreciation for Boston, even as more has emerged about the deterioration of his relationship with Tatum and the organization.

"I love Boston," he said Sunday. "Boston's a great city. A lot of people I developed relationships with, you know what I mean? But I'm just focused on what's in front of me right now. And that's the most important thing."

He also acknowledged everything that accompanies an abrupt end to a decade with one organization.

"Decisions were made," Brown said. "It's life. It's business. Move on. It's OK. … It's emotions. You've got to pack up and move your stuff. Your family's got to pack up and move. But it's life. It's happened to numerous amounts of people, myself included.

"So I just look forward to being able to build with my team over here, trying to make the best of my situation."

Brown faced the Celtics during the preseason, but Tuesday will be the first meeting that counts. He said he did not know whether that would introduce emotions that were absent during the exhibition schedule.

"We'll see how I feel when we get out there," Brown said. "As of now, I've got no emotion toward nothing. So I'm just ready to go."

Tatum was similarly restrained after Boston's 117-97 victory over Milwaukee on Sunday.

"It's another game on the schedule," Tatum said. "It's the Celtics versus the Sixers. In the words of Brad Stevens, they all count as one."

Tatum called the Sixers "an incredible group" with a "great coaching staff," but declined to add to the discussion surrounding his relationship with Brown.

"Drama gets clicks and views," he said. "That's not my thing." CBS Sports reported Tatum's full comments Sunday night.

Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla was even more concise.

"It'll be fun," Mazzulla said. "It'll be a good atmosphere."

Brown is not the only centerpiece of the July deal who will face his former team.

George has settled quickly into Boston's lineup, averaging 20.4 points and supplying the high-volume outside shooting the Celtics have long prioritized. He scored 27 points and made five three-pointers Sunday as Boston beat Milwaukee for its third consecutive victory.

The Celtics have not needed George to duplicate everything Brown provided. He has fit alongside Tatum, Derrick White and Boston's returning core as another willing shooter and versatile defender.

Tatum is averaging 27.1 points, six rebounds and 7.8 assists. His playmaking has been especially important for a team that replaced Brown's downhill pressure with more shooting and ball movement.

Boston enters Tuesday ranked third in offensive rating and fourth in defensive rating. It is one of two NBA teams currently inside the top five on both ends of the floor.

The Celtics have also made 15.6 three-pointers per game, the second-highest average in the league. They set an NBA Cup record by hitting 24 against Charlotte on Friday, then made 18 more Sunday in Milwaukee.

That presents a clear challenge for a Sixers defense that has generally performed well but has occasionally surrendered clean perimeter looks after committing extra help toward the ball. Tatum, George, White, Payton Pritchard and Sam Hauser can all punish late rotations.

The Sixers have reached 9-2 without depending upon the same formula every night.

Tyrese Maxey leads them at 26.9 points per game. Brown is averaging 22.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and four assists while shooting 47.7 percent from the field and 39.2 percent from three. Joel Embiid and LeBron James have supplied scoring, passing and defensive flexibility around them.

Brown has repeatedly described the team as unfinished despite its record.

"From our perspective, it's been some growing pains for sure, even though we've been able to win," he said. "The result, we're not so much fixated on the result. It's more so about the process, and we've got to improve our process and our mentality to creating a winning environment."

Boston should provide the clearest early measure of that process.

The Celtics play considerably slower than the Sixers, but their half-court execution has been more efficient. Philadelphia will want to create turnovers and run before Boston can set its defense. The Celtics will attempt to control the pace, generate three-pointers and make the Sixers execute against a defense that has yet to allow an opposing player to score 30 points this season.

There is also the unavoidable Brown matchup. Boston could use Tatum, George and White against him at different points, giving the Celtics several defenders capable of absorbing his drives without immediately sending help.

Nick Nurse expects Brown to bring something extra, even if Brown has publicly downplayed the emotional component.

"It's going to be very different for him," Nurse said. "I think probably a little bit of emotion in there, too, but also I think he's going to be very motivated to play."

Boston's rotation is healthy entering the matchup. Two-way guard Devin Carter is out because of an illness.

Dominick Barlow and Ariel Hukporti remain out for the Sixers. Adem Bona could return after missing Sunday's contest.

The betting market views the matchup as essentially a toss-up. Monday afternoon listings had the spread moving between Boston minus-1.5 and Philadelphia minus-1.5, depending on the sportsbook, with the total at 215.5.

That fits the larger picture. Philadelphia owns the East's best record. Boston has the conference's strongest point differential and has outscored opponents by 10.7 points per game.

The surrounding conversation will center on Brown and Tatum until the opening tip. Brown does not intend to contribute any ceremonial small talk.

"He's on his side," Brown said. "I'm on my side."

#2739. The top 5 biggest impact deadline trades, including Jaguars and Bears shooting for a Super Bowl

The NFL trade deadline had plenty of action.

There were multiple teams who traded for a new starting quarterback. Stars at all three levels of the defense were dealt. There were well-known offensive linemen and receivers moved. Strangely, after weeks of chatter, the only position that didn't see a trade was running back. But there were enough deals to keep everyone busy.

Here are the five most impactful trades made since the start of this season:

Simmons showed in his first game at Seattle how much he will impact the Bears this season. The Chicago defense looked much different with Simmons in the middle, taking up attention from blockers and still making plays. He was a first-team All-Pro last season and could be on a similar path this season. Everyone had seen how dominant Simmons was, the Bears were just the team that acted on it. They sent two first-round picks to Tennessee for Simmons, who is 29 years old, but the Bears and their fans won't mind if he helps break a Super Bowl drought that dates back to the 1985 season. Given how good Chicago's offense is and how the defense has improved already with Simmons in the middle, it's realistic to think Chicago could find itself in the Super Bowl.

"I think he's just — I don't know — you can feel his presence," linebacker T.J. Edwards said after Simmons' Week 8 Bears debut, according to the team's site. "Especially me, I'm right behind him, so I can kind of just feel how they're trying to block him. I feel like [the defense] was just flying today. They made our job a whole lot easier. But he definitely helps, for sure."

The Eagles had a lot of potential trade chips, but Davis wasn't discussed as one because he was just 26 years old and also one of the highest paid defensive tackles in the NFL. But the Jaguars got aggressive, sending a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick to the Eagles for a player who immediately can replace (and potentially upgrade) from DaVon Hamilton, who was having a tremendous season before he tore his quadriceps and went to injured reserve. It was a very expensive trade, and probably an overpay, but Davis unquestionably makes the Jaguars stronger this season.

The Jaguars also made moves for safety Jessie Bates III and another defensive tackle, Davon Godchaux, but the move for Davis is the big difference-maker for a team that clearly has Super Bowl hopes.

We have to be careful to not overrate the impact of this move. The Vikings still have the fourth-best quarterback and fourth-best offense in their own division. Cousins is 38 years old. And many of the same people who were clamoring for the Vikings to trade for Cousins were the same ones that, during Cousins' previous six seasons in Minnesota, said he could never win anything.

But, it's the kind of move that is very rare in the NFL. Viable starting quarterbacks are rarely available in a trade. The Vikings didn't pay too much, a third-round pick, and it's the rare situation of a quarterback who has played with the coach and in the scheme before. He can step right in. The Vikings have a fantastic defense and now should have a competent offense. Wherever this reunion leads, it was smart for the Vikings to find out.

Hooker is having a career year in his eighth season. He leads the NFL with five interceptions. His Pro Football Focus grade ranks fourth among all NFL safeties with at least 300 snaps. The Bills had a hole at safety after cutting C. J. Gardner-Johnson and did well to land Hooker.

The Bills' defense started slow this season and while it has played well for two weeks, that came against quarterbacks Joe Fagnano and Carson Wentz. Buffalo needed an upgrade on defense. The Bills are pretty good up front, and now they have a potential All-Pro safety this season for the back end. It was a sharp move that should improve the Bills, who are in a great spot to make the Super Bowl for the first time in the Josh Allen era.

When the Giants traded a fifth-round pick for McCarthy, it seemed like a low-cost gamble on a reclamation project. The Giants couldn't have known they had found a starting quarterback for a team that is still in first place of the NFC East. McCarthy had a blistering fourth quarter in relief of Jameis Winston against the Saints, throwing for 243 yards in less than a quarter. He got the starting job after that and the Giants have won both games since.

It's possible McCarthy reverts to the inconsistent form he had last season, which caused the Vikings to give up on the 10th overall pick of the 2024 NFL Draft after only 10 starts. But he has looked poised and gives the Giants a more stable option at quarterback than the hot-and-cold Winston. It seemed like the GIants' season might have been done when Jaxson Dart suffered a knee injury in Week 2, but a smart and cheap trade for McCarthy could end up saving it.

#2732. Tre Johnson is struggling from three. So are the Wizards

DETROIT — Tre Johnson is an elite shooter. It's why the Washington Wizards selected him No. 6 in the 2025 draft. But his jump shot hasn't clicked at the start of the 2026-27 season.

Johnson scored two points on 1-for-8 shooting in Monday's 122-111 loss to the Detroit Pistons just two days after shooting 2-for-15 in a 114-75 loss to the Oklahoma City Thunder. Johnson missed all 13 of his 3-point attempts in those contests.

He is shooting 35.1% from the field through 11 games. His 24.5% 3-point percentage is the second-worst in the NBA among players with at least 50 3-point attempts this season, trailing only Ace Bailey's 22.6%.

In Monday's loss, Johnson missed two wide-open triples — one in the far corner and another on the wing — in the first half. In the second half, he missed three more open looks to finish 0-for-6 from long range. His lone make was a 3-foot push shot that rimmed in.

Johnson is getting open looks. He's just missing them.

We saw what he did last year with the percentage he shot. That'll turn. He puts in all the work, and I got great faith in him."

Johnson's struggles are concerning. But he's far from the only Wizards with an inefficient 3-ball. The Wizards made just nine of their 36 3-point attempts in Monday's loss. They're shooting 29% from three, which ranks 29th in the league.

Trae Young made just three of his 10 3-point attempts in Monday's loss. He's shooting 28.8% from three. Alex Sarr missed both of his outside jumpers to fall to 19.4% from three this season. Kyshawn George shot just 2-for-6 from long range.

Washington has a shooting problem. Keefe believes this slump will pass. But 11 games in, the Wizards' spacing concerns have been realized.

"We've got guys who can make them. I've got faith in our shooters. We're in a tough stretch shooting-wise, but these things will average out," Keefe said. " We're going to continue to do the right things, put ourselves in the position to make those shots, and I got faith in our guys."

AJ Dybantsa, who scored 21 points against Detroit but made just one of his four 3-point attempts, reiterated that sentiment. The rookie remained confident in the Wizards' ability to make open shots, especially from three.

"Keep shooting. We're NBA players. We're gonna knock shots down," Dybantsa said. "We might be in a shooting slump right now, but [we] have to keep shooting."

#2731. Bills offense dominates time of possession, grinds down valiant Vikings defense

Joe Brady likes to say the Buffalo Bills play nameless, faceless opponents.

The Minnesota Vikings can probably say the same, but only because they bring enough heat to peel the faces off opposing offenses, bolstering a high-blitzing phisolsophy by being fast, physical and intelligent.

When someone looks at the statistics down the road, they might think the Bills had an off game. They had season-lows in points (23), total yards (339) and yards per play (4.3) And yet the Vikings allowed season-high 23 points in a 23-6 loss.

There have been times Josh Allen and the Bills have grown frustrated playing small ball, leaning on the run game and resisting the urge to hunt splash plays. Not against the Vikings. They won ugly; they grinded out the win.

The Vikings had only allowed one 80-yard drive all season — a one-play, 81-yard drive against the Green Bay Packers in the first quarter of the season opener — and the Bills produced three, choking out Minnesota by holding the ball over 42 minutes.

"Time of possession is good. Yards is good. It's only good if you're scoring touchdowns," Brady said. "... The guys stuck together and found a way to win. They earned that win. Finding a way is the wrong term, but they earned it."

Typically Josh Allen draws special game plans. Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores just did what he does to everyone: blitz.

The Vikings, who blitz 71% of the time — almost 40 points higher than the league average and 30 points more than the next highest defense — send five or more rushers on 12 of Allen's first 15 drop-backs. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, they blitzed him on 68% of his 35 drop-backs and it was ugly for most of the first half.

The Bills attempted to counter Minnesota's blitz by using six or seven players in pass protection. They had five players run routes just 10 times, the lowest rate of Brady's career as a play-caller. And, at times, it was counterproductive.

While the Vikings sometimes walk eight players to the line of scrimmage, they are most often only sending five. So when the Bills ran three-man routes, they had six players in coverage. Combine that with the Bills struggling to find which five were rushing and Allen was sacked four times, including three in the first half.

Allen started the game 6 of 14 for 52 yards, with a sack squandering a 58-yard game-opening kick return by Greg Dortch and an interception nullifying a second drive, as the Bills got just three points despite having the ball inside the Minnesota 40 on three straight drives to start the game.

But after three previous drives netted a total of minus-3 yards on 11 plays, the Bills got the ball with 4:02 left in the first half. Brady went to the quick passing game and immediately found success, going 80 yards on eight plays.

Allen got into a rhythm, going 6 of 6 for 70 yards. The Vikings finally chose not to blitz and Allen was able to extend the play to find tight end Keleki Latu in the end zone for his first career touchdown catch to take a 10-3 lead.

From that drive, Allen went 15 of 17 for 182 yards, finishing with 234 for the game, which is the most allowed by the Vikings since Green Bay's Jordan Love threw for 387 in Week 1.

"Those guys are coming, they're coming fast," Allen said. "They're so smart on the back end. They're able to read and flow with eyes. … That's a tough defense."

But Brady had decided leading up to the game that the best way to beat the Vikings was to wear them down. He watched the Detroit Lions run for 230 yards and hold the ball for nearly 36 minutes, something he referenced earlier in the week.

It became even more appealing when they ruled out left tackle Dion Dawkins (rib) and left guard Alec Anderson (ankle) before the game. That moved veteran Austin Corbett into the lineup at left guard and Tylan Grable — who made his NFL first start last week at right tackle for Spencer Brown — to left tackle.

Cook didn't have much room to run, totaling just 18 yards on his first 10 carries. In fact, Cook had one run over 10 yards the entire game and it came in the fourth quarter, one play before Cook sealed the game with a 5-yard touchdown run to take a 20-6 lead.

The Bills gobbled 8:32 off the clock and used 15 plays to march 84 yards on that drive, with Cook carrying eight times for 45 yards. He finished with 107 yards on 31 attempts.

It's one thing for an offense to score points — and no team scores more than the Bills — but it's another to use an offense to control the game simply by managing the clock and controlling the tempo.

"Eventually you end up making it a game that they weren't willing to play," Brady said. "That's a good football team and that's a great defense. And to be able to just stay on the field and be able to possess the ball, is really hard. … Really proud of that locker room."

Beck started warming up, but Minshew didn't miss any snaps in the game.

The loss against Seattle was Minshew's first start of the season, after he replaced Jacoby Brissett in the team's comeback overtime win over the Dallas Cowboys. Minshew has thrown for 354 yards with three touchdowns and no interceptions in two games this year.

Minshew's promotion to starter also came after Brissett was traded to the Baltimore Ravens last week.

With Beck as the only other quarterback in Arizona's organization, the team signed career backup Josh Johnson off the Cleveland Browns' practice squad. The Cardinals will be Johnson's 15th NFL team in his 14-year career. Arizona also signed QB Joey Aguilar.

Beck has not yet played in a regular season game. The rookie played extensively in Arizona's first preseason action against the Carolina Panthers in the Hall of Fame Game.

The quarterback completed 15 of 19 passes for 188 yards and a touchdown, with no interceptions, in the loss to the Panthers. Beck suffered a rib injury during the game that sidelined him for the rest of the preseason.

Minshew isn't the only potential season-ending injury that Arizona is dealing with. Wide receiver Michael Wilson fractured something in his neck, according to head coach Mike LaFleur, and will miss the remainder of the season.

The Cardinals play the Los Angeles Rams this week. Arizona then has the Kansas City Chiefs, Washington Commanders and Philadelphia Eagles, then a Week 14 bye.

Arizona is 3-6 and last in the NFC West. With the trade decisions made earlier in the year and the high-profile injuries suffered last week, the rest of the season may be an evaluation of the team's young talent.

Here are five fantasy trends grabbing my attention heading into Week 4 of the fantasy basketball season, plus some rapid-fire notes on every other team.

Heat: One of the bigger surprises has been Miami's Davion Mitchell, who's ranked inside the top 55 in both 9-cat and standard points leagues, outpacing his ADP of 118.7. The steals he's piling up (over 2 per contest) are what's driving most of his rise up the ranks. He's playing a ton of minutes while keeping his turnovers down and delivering a versatile 9-4-4 line with almost 3 steals a night. There's some sell-high appeal here, especially in 9-cat leagues. In 42% of Dunn trades, he's part of a package deal, so you'll likely have to include someone else to make a swap.

Timberwolves: Let's not gloss over Minnesota's Jaden McDaniels, who is crushing his ADP (ranked 46th in 9-cat after going 89th on draft day). Through 11 games, he's on pace for career-bests in minutes, points, rebounds, assists, 3s and usage per game. That's a massive offensive responsibility for a rookie, and the Kings' 1-9 start gives them little reason to limit his development. His scoring (25.9 ppg) and assists (7.4 apg) make him especially appealing in points leagues. Although, even with his warts in inefficiency and turnovers, he's in the top 80 in 9-cat, well above his preseason ADP.

Bucks: In Milwaukee, Brayden Burries has overtaken Ryan Rollins in the starting lineup. Burries is averaging 13 points, 8.3 rebounds and 3.5 assists across three starts. That rebounding from a guard is particularly appealing in category leagues, and the Bucks' 1-9 start should give Burries an opportunity to establish himself. He is one of my priority adds this week.

Hawks: Atlanta has made a similar move to Milwaukee, starting rookie Kingston Flemings over CJ McCollum. Flemings is gaining valuable playing time and experience, while McCollum's fantasy outlook remains stable, operating in a timeshare and sixth man role. The Hawks have a 124 Offensive Rating with Flemings running point (small sample but a good signal nonetheless). His shot volume and efficiency have improved over that three-game span, too — now, let's see if it'll hold and if he can generate more potential assists.

Thunder: Rookie Aday Mara offers immediate appeal as a shot-blocking specialist. The rim protection, plus rebounding, give him a useful 9-cat profile. Coming off the best performance of his young career over the weekend (18 points with 8 rebounds and 3 blocks), Mara will have to earn every chance to sustain a 20-25 minute role nightly.

#2726. ‘There’s lots of things about that program that are fantastic’: Arizona coach Brent Brennan previews big-time matchup vs. Utah

Arizona is preparing for its biggest game of the season, and coach Brent Brennan wants to see a full house.

The Wildcats have yet to sell out the 50,782-seat Casino Del Sol Stadium this season, and haven't sold out the stadium since a 2024 game against Colorado, per Tucson.com writer Justin Spears.

With No. 3 Utah in town, Fox pregame show Big Noon Kickoff broadcasting live from Tucson and a 5:30 p.m. MST kickoff, Brennan is ready to see Tucson show up to support the No. 22 Wildcats.

"This is the game to show up for your alma mater, to show up for your university or show up for this city and how this institution is wired into the city of Tucson," Brennan said at his weekly press conference.

"... Let's show everybody how freaking dope the city of Tucson is. Let's show them what this institution, the University of Arizona, is all about by going absolutely nuts."

Brennan pointed to the atmosphere at Rice-Eccles Stadium in Utah's 28-20 win over BYU as a bit of inspiration for the Arizona home crowd.

"It looked fantastic. Yeah, it looked great. I've coached in a bunch of games there over the course of my career as an assistant and as a head coach and they have a great game day," Brennan said. "You could see that it had an impact on BYU at times in that game, and that's what I'm talking about here in Casino Del Sol Stadium on Saturday night. Our fan base, the Zona Zoo, our alums, the city making that incredibly challenging for Utah."

The stakes are especially high for Arizona, which is 4-2 in Big 12 play. The Wildcats need an upset win over the undefeated Utes to remain in the Big 12 title race and have a still have a chance at making the College Football Playoff.

For Utah, a victory not only preserves an undefeated season, but moves the Utes one win away from clinching their first-ever spot in the Big 12 championship game in the event's final year of operation.

Whether the atmosphere turns out to be formidable or not, the Utes are facing a formidable opponent in Arizona. Add in the fact that the Utes have to hit the road following an emotional rivalry win over No. 9 BYU last week, and it's going to require everything Utah has to come out of Tucson with a win.

Quarterback Noah Fifita has had Utah's number in the last two meetings — a 42-18 loss that was the low point of the Utes' 2023 season and a 23-10 loss in 2024. Utah's defense will be tested once again by a fast-paced, explosive offense led by a good quarterback.

Fifita is fourth in the nation in passing yards this season (2,794) and has one of the nation's highest explosive pass percentages (7.8% of his pass plays result in a gain of 30 or more yards, per Hudl IQ).

Utah has given up explosive passing plays in nearly every Big 12 game, and has allowed 233.8 passing yards per game, ranking No. 102 in FBS. Yet it's tough to bet against the Utes' defense after what they've shown through the first nine games, including wins against top-15 opponents BYU and Houston.

Utah's red-zone defense has been stellar, and despite giving up a lot of passing yards, the Utes rank No. 15 in the nation in points per game with 16.3. Utah has also intercepted opposing quarterbacks 13 times, tied for No. 4 in the country.

"They're super good on defense, incredibly good in the red zone. And so it's going to be a physical, physical game and that's what it is every time you play Utah," Brennan said.

Quarterback Devon Dampier and Utah's offense, however, dominated the talk in Brennan's press conference.

Dampier registered four touchdowns in Utah's win over BYU, two of which were rushing scores. The dual-threat senior presents a big challenge for Arizona's defense.

"That's kryptonite in all of football. Who are the best quarterbacks in the NFL? All the guys that can move. So guys that they're able to utilize plus-one run game or escape these incredibly athletic, twitchy defensive linemen," Brennan said.

"So I think that's a challenge for all of college football and obviously Dampier is exceptional at it."

Arizona will hope to contain Dampier's rushing abilities, but Brennan is not tipping his game plan, obviously.

"We're getting ready to play the No. 2 team in the country. I'm not going to give you anything schematically or how are we going to slow down this incredible player, right?" Brennan said. "But we're going to do everything we can to do it. And they combine that with a great running game. They got receivers that can make plays. They got a bunch of big tight ends. Their O-line is massive and athletic and tough."

Brennan is familiar with Utah's offensive brain trust in offensive coordinator Kevin McGiven and quarterbacks coach Ryan Gunderson, working with the pair at both Oregon State and San Jose State. He also worked with Utah safeties coach Derrick Odum at San Jose State.

"Those guys are really good people and really good football coaches. The success they're having doesn't surprise me because I believe in those guys," Brennan said.

Brennan has coached against Scalley as a defensive coordinator a number of times, both as a head coach and assistant coach, but Saturday will be the first time facing off against Scalley as a head coach.

Brennan has a lot of respect for Utah's program heading into Saturday night's big-time matchup.

"There's lots of things about that program that are fantastic. There's been a consistency there. They've played in the Rose Bowl. They've won the conference. I know it was the old conference (Pac-12), but they've done a great job since moving from the Mountain West into the Power Four," Brennan said.

"I got a ton of respect for what they do there. Coach Scalley's doing a great job. They're very well-coached. Three guys that I worked with over the course of my career are coaching on that staff there. I love those guys. I believe in them. I'm happy for them and I'm excited for this big-time matchup on Saturday night."

#2720. Falcons steal K Jake Moody from Ravens’ practice squad

The Baltimore Ravens need a new kicker. Again.

The Atlanta Falcons are signing Jake Moody off of the Ravens' practice squad, per NFL insider Jordan Schultz, robbing Baltimore of another kicker less than a week after Week 1 starter Tyler Loop landed on injured reserve with a groin injury.

The move raises questions about the Ravens' approach to their kicker situation with Loop sidelined for at least four games. The team had a roster spot available, but opted to elevate Moody from the practice squad to face the Jacksonville Jaguars last Thursday. With only two elevations remaining, he would have required a promotion to the 53-man roster to see out Loop's absence, which would have also precluded his departure to Atlanta. Logic suggests that the Ravens should have just promoted Moody knowing they would need him to kick for the rest of the month, maybe longer.

Additional reporting from Jeff Zrebiec of The Athletic indicated that the Ravens were "willing" to promote Moody to their active roster on Monday. The Falcons, though, offered a better situation after releasing kicker Jason Sanders: a potential long-term job for Moody and a home field enclosed by a dome.

It still seems, though, that Baltimore could have headed off this entire issue had they promoted Moody to the active roster last week. It is possible that his agent was keeping tabs on the Falcons' kicking situation and preferred a practice squad stay to preserve his options. However, Loop has not exactly inspired much confidence that he can deliver key kicks for a team that will need to win at the margins to make the playoffs this year. There is an argument that the Ravens should have identified Moody as their kicker for the foreseeable future and adjusted their roster accordingly.

Instead, they will have to scour the NFL's practice squads and free-agent pool to find their next kicker. Signing Nick Folk, who the Falcons cut to add Moody, would be an ironic twist. After three straight years of leading the league with a field goal conversion rate of 95.5% or better, the 42-year-old's numbers have collapsed in 2026. He made just 72.2% of his field goals to start the season with two misses inside of 50 yards and a one-for-four mark from beyond.

The Bees had to beat the Football League's basement side Crawley Town in their final fixture in Southern Group H to progress and did so courtesy of a Domeiro Bobb-Semple double in a 2-1 success at Broadfield Stadium, where Connor Wickham scored on his Crawley debut.

In Southern Group B, the Foxes trailed at the King Power Stadium against League Two Walsall, who would have gone through in place of their hosts with a win. But strikes from Will Smallbone and John Lundstram put them ahead by the break and they held on.

Stevenage topped the group by beating Fulham U21 on penalties.

Chelsea U21 were not in action but went through at the expense of Reading, who needed a big win away against Bristol Rovers to see them overtake the west London side in Southern Group C, but the Royals were beaten on penalties.

Nottingham Forest U21 and Notts County both eased through into the last 16 with wins in Northern Group F.

Forest enjoyed a 3-0 success against League Two promotion-chasers Grimsby Town at Blundell Park, where all the goals came before the break.

Domeiro Bobb-Semple (right) scored a goal in each half for the Bees youngsters [Getty Images]

Oxford United coasted to a 4-0 win over Cheltenham Town to pip the Robins to the runners-up spot in Southern Group A.

In Southern Group G, Gillingham made sure of their place in the last 16 by seeing off Northampton Town 2-1. Seb Campbell crashed home a 99th-minute winner as Plymouth Argyle beat Swindon Town at Home Park to finish top of the pile in Southern Group E, while Colchester United beat Ipswich Town U21 on penalties after a 0-0 draw in Southern Group D, in a match where both sides knew their campaign had ended after their second fixture.

Elsewhere, a close-range shot by Tom Graves put Crewe Alexandra on track for the win they needed to progress from Northern Group B, but Wigan Athletic scored twice in the second half to dash their hopes, while veteran forward Nick Powell was among the scorers as Bradford City thumped York City 4-0 to top Northern Group C.

In a thriller in Northern Group D, already eliminated Mansfield Town looked set for their first points of the competition as they led already qualified Chesterfield 3-1 with 28 minutes remaining. But Dylan Duffy scored two of four goals in the closing stages to earn the Spireites a remarkable 5-3 victory.

Stockport County beat Tranmere Rovers on penalties in Northern Group E, but both sides were already sure of qualification, while Huddersfield Town thumped Liverpool U21 4-0 to finish top of Northern Group H.

#2716. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2712. Jamie Little Stepping Away From The Booth, Will Focus on Pit Road Duties in 2027

FOX NASCAR reporter Jamie Little announced on Tuesday that she will shift her focus away from play-by-play commentary beginning next year. Little intends to prioritize her role as a NASCAR on FOX pit reporter in the Cup Series, as well as select IndyCar Series races.

For the last six years, Little has expanded her role at FOX as the lead play-by-play announcer for the Craftsman Truck Series and the ARCA Menards Series. FS1, the FOX sports channel owned by the FOX corporation, is the exclusive home of both the Truck Series and ARCA Menards Series.

Little has been a pit reporter for NASCAR since 2007 for a number of different networks, including ABC, ESPN, and FOX.

On social media, Little put out a post making her intentions known for 2027. The pit reporter said she is "changing things up a bit" next year. Little, a wife and mother of two, would like to devote more of her time to her family in 2027.

Because of this, Little said her commitments to both being a pit reporter in the Cup Series and a play-by-play announcer for NASCAR's lower-level series is too time-consuming. Little is appreciative of every opportunity FOX has given her and appreciates her time in the booth.

Here is the statement Little put out via social media:

"Starting next season, my focus will be on the NASCAR Cup Series pit road and select IndyCar races. My kids are still young and deserve more of my time."

"Thank you to everyone who has watched and supported my journey as a play-by-play voice for ARCA and the Truck Series the last six years. It's been quite a ride and one I'll always be thankful to have experienced. A special thank you to FOX for always giving me opportunities."

FOX Sports, which has broadcasted NASCAR Cup Series races since 2001, will once again be the exclusive home for the first slate of Cup Series races in 2027. The season will kick off with the Daytona 500, NASCAR's most prestigious race, which FOX has broadcasted every year since 2007.

Longtime play-by-play announcer Mike Joy, soon-to-be NASCAR Hall of Famer Kevin Harvick, and retired NASCAR driver Clint Bowyer are all expected to return to the FOX booth next year.

FOX Sports will air the first 12 Cup Series points-paying races in 2027 and wrap up its slate with the All-Star exhibition at North Wilkesboro in May.

#2711. Colts keep RB Jonathan Taylor at NFL trade deadline, reportedly turned down offers of second-round picks

The Indianapolis Colts were aggressive sellers at the trade deadline.

But the most prominent potential trade piece on their roster is staying put. Per NFL Insider Tom Pelissero, the Colts declined to trade three-time Pro Bowl running back Jonathan Taylor ahead of Tuesday's NFL trade deadline.

Per the report, Indianapolis turned down multiple offers of second-round picks to keep Taylor in a Colts uniform. The Colts would have only considered a "blockbuster" return to part with Taylor, according to the report.

It's a curious decision for a team that's given up on the season and faces what looks like a long road back to relevance.

Taylor has been one of the league's most reliable and productive backs throughout his seven-season NFL career. At 27 years old — toward the end of the traditional running-back prime — he's a potential difference-maker for a team seeking to compete for a championship now. The Colts are not that and don't project to be anytime soon.

But Taylor has been the face of the Colts through most of his career and is a fan favorite. That holds value in Indianapolis, so much that the Colts reportedly turned down multiple reasonable offers that would have provided a valuable asset to build for the future.

Amid the failures of extending Daniel Jones and trading two first-round picks for Sauce Gardner, the Colts fired longtime general manager Chris Ballard in October after a 2-4 start. This triggered a fire sale in Indianapolis that featured the trades of All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson and former Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner on the same day on Oct. 27.

Indianapolis continued its roster purge Tuesday with the trade of wide receiver Keenan Allen to the 49ers as the trade deadline approached. Hours later, the Colts reportedly agreed to trade wide receiver Josh Downs to the Chiefs.

But Taylor is reportedly staying put alongside Jones on an offense that looks little like it did when the Colts started the season with hopes of competing for the playoffs.

#2706. Lakers ‘registered interest’ in Nique Clifford before trade to Thunder

On Sunday afternoon, the Sacramento Kings agreed to deal second-year wing Nique Clifford to the Oklahoma City Thunder in exchange for two second-round picks. Clifford held a fairly sizable role during his rookie season, when he averaged 8.6 points, 3.8 rebounds, 2.4 assists and 0.9 steals in 25.1 minutes per game.

But he'd fallen out of Sacramento's rotation to begin 2026-27 and played just 50 minutes in eight games prior to the trade. With the Thunder ravaged by early season injuries, they opted to tap into their surplus of picks and add a reinforcement to their wing room with the hopes he might break out in a more stable organization.

Oklahoma City, however, was not the lone playoff hopeful eyeing Clifford. Marc Stein and Jake Fischer reported that a trio of other suitors, including the Los Angeles Lakers, gauged the market for him. Ultimately, though, the Thunder emerged victorious in the Nique Clifford Sweepstakes.

"The Pacers, Nuggets and Lakers, sources say, were among the teams that registered trade interest in the 24-year-old," according to The Stein Line Substack, "but Oklahoma City had multiple advantages when it came to getting a deal done."

Among the "multiple advantages" referenced there is presumably Oklahoma City's wealth of picks. Between 2027 and 2033, it owns 15 second-round picks, one of which is Los Angeles' 2032 second-rounder. For comparison, the Lakers own just three over that same span.

Plus, the Lakers are also already fairly well-stocked with youthful wings worth taking a swing on this season. Adou Thiero (22 years old), Cameron Carr (22) and Ziaire Williams (25) are all 25 or younger and have garnered varying levels of rotation minutes to open the year. Given the Lakers' depleted well of draft capital, it probably didn't make much sense to fork over two of their remaining three second-round picks through 2033 for a dude who *might* crack the rotation on certain nights.

If they're going to move some of those picks, it should be for someone they know can be a difference-maker and mainstay in the rotation. Clifford, while still pretty young and far from a finished product in the league, certainly does not fit that billing.

#2705. Grading the trade: Josh Downs gives Chiefs WR help they needed, but is he the right fit?

Just prior to the trade deadline, the Kansas City Chiefs acquired wide receiver Josh Downs from the Indianapolis Colts. The Chiefs will receive Downs and a 2027 seventh-round pick, and the Colts will get back fourth- and fifth-round picks in 2027.

Downs, 25, who recently requested a trade, got his wish and now will team up with Patrick Mahomes. In nine games (seven starts) with the Colts this season, Downs caught 33 passes for 354 yards and one TD on 57 targets.

Downs also had a team-high seven catches for 72 yards on nine targets in the Colts' 33-30 loss in Kansas City back in Week 2.

Who won this trade? Let's dive into the debate.

The Chiefs were in big need of adding receiver help. Not one wideout on the roster has either 50 targets or 300 yards receiving on the season. Downs, sharing the lead role in Indy along with Keenan Allen (and with Alec Pierce hurt), has surpassed both marks.

That's not to say that he instantly will become Patrick Mahomes' go-to target. But it's hard not to imagine Downs stepping in and earning a fairly sizable role in Kansas City's offense, assuming he can develop a relationship with Mahomes and pick up the playbook quickly.

Downs has primarily been a slot receiver in his career, although his work rate playing outside has increased slightly in 2026 out of need. It would make sense to put him in the slot, although what makes him, Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy attractive is that they can line up in multiple spots.

Rice's numbers over the past year-plus have been slightly better inside, but Worthy has been far more efficient as a perimeter receiver in his career. That likely means Downs can take those snaps and do what he does best: run efficient routes, separate quickly and generate first downs. The biggest drawback is that Downs is not a deep threat, which was probably their biggest need.

This move also can help the Chiefs' punt-return situation. Nikko Remigio has struggled in that role this season. Downs has only returned two punts this season, but he has a very respectable 9.8-yard career average on punt returns.

The Chiefs know that Downs is a free agent after the season, and they had to be comfortable with the idea of this trade potentially being a half-season rental. Thinning out their Day 3 pick allotment stings a little, but the price wasn't that steep in the big picture, especially when you compare it to what the Seahawks paid for Rashid Shaheed (fourth- and fifth-round picks) and what the Jaguars dealt for Jakobi Meyers (fourth- and sixth-rounders) before last year's deadline.

This move is about taking advantage of a championship window with Mahomes showing he's recovered from his knee injury and Travis Kelce still performing at a relatively high level in his expected swan-song season.

Downs requested a trade and got his wish. The Colts likely weren't convinced they had to extend him, and Downs probably wasn't returning to Indianapolis next season anyway, so trading him now made perfect sense instead of waiting for compensatory-pick returns more than a year from now.

It fits right in line with the other trades they've made since firing GM Chris Ballard, shipping out one-time franchise pillars Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner and also dealing Allen. When you consider what they got back for Downs, which was two early Day 3 picks, it was a pretty fair market price.

Not having a first-rounder next spring from the Sauce Gardner will continue to sting. But with the trades, they've managed to replenish the cupboard a bit. They already have seven Day 3 picks to work with and are projected to receive two more compensatory selections in that same range.

Having those picks can allow the Colts potentially to slide up in the draft, and quarterback could be on the menu given the uncertainty surrounding Daniel Jones, even if Jones was not traded by the deadline.

They'll also eventually need to replenish a gutted WR room, but for now the Colts can see what they have in the likes of Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, Anthony Gould, Ashton Dulin, Deion Burks, Laquon Treadwell and, of course, Pierce, when he's back healthy again. It wouldn't be stunning if the Colts only bring back a few of these players next year, but the remainder of the season will help them decide who stays and who goes.

#2704. Lanning: Stewart incident 'didn't match our standard'

EUGENE — After Oregon wide receiver Evan Stewart was booked in Springfield Municipal Jail early Sunday morning on DUII charges, Ducks coach Dan Lanning addressed the situation at his weekly press conference Monday.

"There was an incident this weekend that didn't match our standard here in our program," Lanning said. "There will be an appropriate action taken. Still gathering some details with what that situation looks like. But that would be handled internally. I'm not gonna respond to any other questions about that. We're gonna handle that with our guys.

"There's an expectation of what you have to... how you have to act, and how you need to perform in our program. Kind of overshadows the success that we had on Saturday, which is disappointing, but that will be handled by us internally. I'm not going to speak on it publicly."

When Lanning was asked a follow-up question about a rumored speeding incident involving other Oregon football players, for which there haven't been any confirmed arrests, he said, "I was talking about the same thing when I first addressed it."

This is also the second instance of an Oregon football team member facing DUII charges in the past year. In April, running backs coach Ra'Shaad Samples allegedly backed his Ford F-150 into a parked car outside a bar in Eugene. His next court date is Oct. 27.

An arraignment for Stewart in his DUII case hasn't been set, as official charges haven't been filed to Springfield Municipal Court as of Monday evening, according to court records.

Stewart leads the Ducks this season with 27 catches for 352 yards and four touchdowns. He missed Saturday's win over Nebraska due to an undisclosed injury.

Oregon (4-2, 2-1 Big Ten) is preparing for a road game at Illinois (3-3, 1-2) at 12 p.m. PT this coming Saturday.

#2701. Cardinals place QB Gardner Minshew and WR Michael Wilson on IR

The Cardinals placed quarterback Gardner Minshew and wide receiver Michael Wilson on injured reserve Tuesday, the team announced.

Minshew tore the UCL in his elbow and will miss the rest of the season. Wilson’s neck injury will end his season.

“Not the ending I had envisioned, but grateful for the journey,” Wilson wrote on social media. “Regardless of what happens, my love for the game will never change! Thank you for all the love and support. The story is still being written.”

Wilson played eight games in 2026, making 51 receptions for 546 yards and two touchdowns.

In two appearances, Minshew completed 38 of 53 passes for 354 yards and three touchdowns, and led the Cardinals to an overtime win in Dallas in Week 8. He is scheduled to be a free agent at the end of the season.

The Cardinals signed veteran quarterback Josh Johnson and rookie quarterback Joey Aguilar to back up rookie Carson Beck. Beck will get his first NFL start on Sunday against the Rams.

Aguilar was on the Jaguars’ practice squad, and Johnson was on the Bengals’ practice squad.

The Cardinals also signed receiver Phillip Dorsett II to the practice squad and released tight end Rivaldo Fairweather and running back Jermar Jefferson from the practice squad.

#2700. Paul George treating return to Philly as “a regular game”

Lost in the background of the highly anticipated first matchup between Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum is a return to Philadelphia for Paul George, who spent his past two seasons as a Sixer.

Both Brown and Tatum have downplayed the narrative, as hard as it is to ignore. George, who played 89 games in a Sixers uniform, is following suit.

"It's a regular game — that's how I'm treating it," he said during Boston's morning shootaround.

George said he was unsure of the reception he'd receive in his first game back to Xfinity Mobile Arena, a place where in his last appearance, he scored a series-best 23 points on 47% efficiency to go with vintage defense, forcing four Celtics turnovers and holding shooters matched up with him to 33% (5/15 FG). It played a part in Philly completing the 14th 3-1 series comeback in NBA history.

And yet, George's brief stint in Philadelphia was defined by a core group that struggled to stay on the floor at the same time, and ran into the same second round demons they've yet to exorcise since the beginning of The Process.

"Had I been here 8, 9, 10 years it'd be a different story. I was there 2 years," he said.

It's an easy narrative to shrug off for George because, over his 17 seasons, he's gone through this same thing before.

"He said he's returned to four different teams before. There's nothing new to him," Payton Pritchard said.

George had his own contentious reunion when he played against the Indiana Pacers for the first time, followed by games against the Thunder and Clippers.

George isn't the only Celtic currently on the roster to have experienced an anticipated reunion between a foundational player and the team that drafted him.

Mike Conley, a 12-year Grizzlies mainstay before the organization ended the Grit and Grind with a full scale rebuild, was showered with appreciation and given a hero's welcome from the Memphis fanbase in his first game against them in 2019.

Their experiences couldn't have been farther apart.

In the case of George, whose seven years in Indiana ended in a trade request, he first played the Pacers in Oklahoma City, struggling with foul trouble and playing just 19 minutes in an 18-point win. When he played in Indiana for the first time later that season, he was showered with boos from the moment his name was announced, and he shot just 3-of-14 for 12 points, though a late steal and two clutch free throws contributed to a 100-95 win.

"I'm happy this circus is over with. Everybody can move on," George said after his return to Indiana.

The response was different in George's next stop; he was given a tribute video and crowd ovation playing against the Thunder for the first time. Against the Clippers, a video tribute was also presented, but there was a mix of cheers and boos, a reaction he described as "stupid," though he cited no ill will towards the franchise or his time spent in Los Angeles.

"The boos, I didn't get it," he said after his first game against the Clippers. "I still don't get it when I go [back] to Indy, but it is what it is. It's sports. I look forward to next year being back here and more boos."

It's hard to say the exact response when George's name is called in the lineup introductions tonight. As the Celtics got rolling on their shootaround inside Xfinity Mobile Arena, the song "Why Can't We Be Friends" by War blared from the speakers, a tongue and cheek choice to kick off what will be one of the most watched and debated rivalry games of the season.

Perhaps it's a sign that tempers will be calm on Tuesday night. The game will be played, hands will be shaken, and hugs will be dispersed from competitor to competitor after an early November test between two Eastern Conference contenders.

#2699. Who will call plays for Oregon after Mehringer's firing?

EUGENE — After firing first-year offensive coordinator Drew Mehringer seven games into the 2026 season, Dan Lanning shared Oregon's plans for filling his role moving forward at his weekly press conference Monday night.

Offensive assistant Jay Johnson will lead offensive playcalling for the Ducks going forward, Lanning said.

"He has a lot of experience as a play-caller, was with me in Georgia when we were part of the national championship team," Lanning said. "Went on to have a lot of success in Colorado and Michigan State. He's gonna lead the efforts there with the offensive staff, but it'll still be a collaborative effort, with a lot of the work that we do.

"He's also coming in with a different perspective, a different view, not being with us the last few years, where he can provide a couple things that might be different than what we've done."

Mehringer, previously the tight ends coach for the Ducks, is the first assistant coach Lanning has fired in his tenure at Oregon, which began in 2022. The Ducks' offensive decision-making was at the center of intense criticism over the past three weeks, during which Oregon averaged just 14 points per game and lost twice to UCLA and Illinois.

Lanning spoke to the human element of letting Mehringer go.

"They see the football coach, right? That's also an unbelievable dad. A great husband," Lanning said. "The guy's been part of our staff for the last five years, that's done some really good things here, and I think all of us feel like we shoulder some of the blame. Because we didn't create success for our team this season."
